docs.title: Intuit Tank
docs.text:
Intuit Tank is an open-source load test platform. You record or write scripts, group them into projects, and Tank runs them from on-demand agents, usually EC2 instances in AWS. It reports response times and throughput while the test runs.

Tank is built for load testing. You can use it for functional checks, but it lacks many of the tools a functional test suite usually needs.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Tank has two parts: a controller and one or more agents.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
The controller is the control plane. It is a single web application, tank.war, that runs on Apache Tomcat and serves:

Path What it is / The web UI (React). /classic/ The original JSF/PrimeFaces UI. It moved here from the root in Tank 5.0.0. /v2/... The REST API (Spring MVC). See Using the REST API.

The controller stores projects, scripts, filters, data file metadata, jobs and users in MySQL. It starts agents, sends them their configuration and test files, and tracks them while a test runs.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Agents generate the load. The controller starts them on demand for a test and terminates them when the test ends, so you pay only for the time the test runs. An agent receives the settings file, the test script and any support files from the controller, and then reports its status and results back.

You can also run long-lived standalone agents on machines you manage, with the controller set not to start EC2 instances. See Standalone deployment.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Browser / REST client
            │  HTTP(S) :8080
            ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────┐        JDBC (jdbc/watsDS)     ┌─────────┐
 │ Controller (tank.war)   │──────────────────────────────▶│  MySQL  │
 │ Tomcat 11               │                               └─────────┘
 │  /         React UI     │──── data files, agent jars ──▶ S3 or local disk
 │  /classic  JSF UI       │──── EC2 RunInstances ───────▶ agent instances
 │  /v2       REST API     │◀─── CloudWatch metrics ────── (Agent Tracker, results)
 └─────────┬───────────────┘
           │ HTTP + WebSocket to agent-port (default 8090)
           ▼                      ▲ REST calls to /v2/agent/... (settings, status, results)
 ┌─────────────────────────┐      │
 │ Agents (EC2 or standalone)────┘
 └─────────────────────────┘
Piece What Tank uses it for Java The build targets Java 21 (maven.compiler.release in the root pom.xml). The project badge lists Java 21 and 25, and the CloudFormation templates in aws-config/ install a Java 25 runtime. Apache Tomcat Hosts the controller. The build compiles against Tomcat 11.0.x, and the aws-config/ template installs Tomcat 11. The project badge also lists Tomcat 10.1. MySQL The controller's database, reached through the JNDI data source jdbc/watsDS. Hibernate creates and updates the tables on startup and keeps audit history (Envers) in *_version tables. The CloudFormation template creates an RDS MySQL 8.4 instance. Amazon EC2 Agent instances, started with the AWS SDK for Java v2. Tank tags each agent with Name, Controller (the controller's instance-name), JobId and JobName, plus any tags you configure. Elastic IPs can be bound to agents. Amazon S3 Optional storage for data files and agent support files (any storage setting that starts with s3:), and an optional results store. Amazon CloudWatch The default results store: response-time and count metrics go to the Intuit/Tank namespace. The controller also reads the agents' CPU, memory and JVM metrics from CloudWatch for the Agent Tracker. The templates install the CloudWatch agent to ship logs and host metrics. AWS X-Ray Optional request tracing. The controller template runs Tomcat with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry Java agent. AWS SSM Parameter Store Optional: the agent AMI ID (ssm-ami) and the OIDC client secret can be read from parameters.

Other results stores (DynamoDB, S3, Wavefront, Graphite) and an OIDC single sign-on provider can be configured in the settings file.

No message queue

Older guides describe ActiveMQ/JMS between the controller and agents. Current Tank has no message queue: the controller and agents talk over HTTP and WebSocket only.

docs.title: Administration
docs.text: Members of the admin group see Admin in the menu bar. The admin section has two pages: Users and Logs.

docs.title: Users
docs.text: Admin › Users lists every user with their email, groups, API token (its last characters, if they have one) and when they last signed in. Search by name or email, sort by column and page through the list.

docs.title: Adding a user
docs.text:
1. Click New user.
  2. Enter the Name, Email and a Password (twice).
  3. Choose the user's Groups. The default groups are marked (default).
  4. Click Create.

A user's name can't change later: it's how Tank records what they own. Users who sign in through SSO for the first time are created automatically, with the default groups.

docs.title: Editing a user
docs.text:
Click Edit on a user's row to:

  • change their email or set a new password (leave it empty to keep the current one);
  • change their groups, which decide what they can do (see Roles and permissions);
  • create, replace or delete their API token. A new token is shown once, so give it to the user straight away.

docs.title: Other actions
docs.text:
• Reset preferences puts every table back to its default columns and widths for that user.
  • Delete removes a user. Their scripts, filters and data files are kept, with their name removed. A user who owns projects can't be deleted until the projects have been given to someone else (change each project's Owner) or deleted. You can't delete yourself.

docs.title: Inactive users
docs.text:
The controller can delete (anonymize) users who haven't signed in for a set time. It checks once, when it starts. Set these at the top level of settings.xml:

Setting Default Description user-auto-deletion-enabled false When false, the controller only logs which users it would delete. user-auto-deletion-retention-days 730 Days without signing in before a user is deleted. user-auto-deletion-permitted-users Comma-separated user names that are never deleted. The admin user is never deleted.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Admin › Logs reads the controller's log files. Logs are read from the controller that answers the request, which may be one of several.

  1. Choose a log file.
  2. Set the Initial lines to read from the end of the file (0 reads the whole file) and how often to read new lines (Refresh every, in seconds; 0 reads once).
  3. Click Load log.

The log opens in a workspace where you can:

  • search events, with filters such as level:error job:123 -logger:Hibernate;
  • show All levels, Warn+ or Errors only;
  • narrow by facets: job, agent instance, transaction, event type and logger;
  • switch between a Timeline of events, Patterns (similar messages grouped, to spot repeated noise) and the Raw text;
  • open an event to see the events around it;
  • copy selected or visible events, or export them as a compact summary or JSON lines, with secrets optionally redacted, to paste into an issue or an LLM.

docs.title: Log level
docs.text: Log level sets the controller's log level (OFF, FATAL, ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG, TRACE or ALL) for every logger. It applies only to the controller that answers, and only until it restarts. INFO is the default.

docs.title: Do I need to run Tank in AWS?
docs.text: No, but Tank is designed for it. Without AWS, run the controller in standalone mode: set <standalone>true</standalone> and start standalone agents on machines you manage, which register with the controller. Keep data files on local disk, and use the REST results reporter or another results store that doesn't need AWS. The Quickstart sets up a local controller this way.

docs.title: Can I use my own MySQL server instead of RDS?
docs.text: Yes. Tank works with any MySQL 8 server it can reach through the jdbc/watsDS data source; the CloudFormation template uses RDS MySQL 8.4. If you don't use RDS, arrange your own backups so you don't lose your projects and scripts if the server fails.

docs.title: Maven runs out of memory when I build Tank
docs.text:
Give Maven more memory before you build:

export MAVEN_OPTS="$MAVEN_OPTS -Xms2g -Xmx3g"

Appending keeps any options you already set in MAVEN_OPTS, such as a trust store.

docs.title: How do I sign in for the first time?
docs.text:
When the controller starts, it creates each user listed under security/users in settings.xml that doesn't exist yet. The default file creates admin with the password admin, in the admin group. Sign in with those and change the password straight away.

To use a different first password, change the entry before the controller's first start. Once the user exists, Tank doesn't update it from settings.xml, so later edits there have no effect: change the password in the UI instead.

If single sign-on is configured, users can also sign in through your identity provider.

docs.title: Where is the settings file?
docs.text: Tank reads settings.xml from the controller's working directory, or from the folder named by the WATS_PROPERTIES environment variable or system property. If there isn't one, Tank writes the default file there on first start. See Configuration.

docs.title: Where did the old UI go?
docs.text: Since Tank 5.0.0 the React UI is at the root of the controller, and the original JSF UI is at /classic/, for example http://localhost:8080/classic/.

docs.title: How do I call the REST API from a script?
docs.text: Create an API token for your user and send it as Authorization: Bearer <token>. See Using the REST API.

docs.title: My agents start but the test never runs
docs.text:
The controller's watchdog relaunches agents that don't report in time (max-time-for-agent-report, 3 minutes by default) and stops the job after max-restarts attempts. Check that:

  • Agents can reach the controller at controller-base-url.
  • The controller can reach agents on the agent port, TCP 8090 by default (agent-port).
  • The agent AMI's architecture matches the instance types. The default instance types are Graviton (arm64).
  • When rest-security-enabled is true, agent-token is set.
  • The agent logs, in /opt/tank_agent/logs/agent.log on the agent (and in CloudWatch Logs if you installed the CloudWatch agent), show what failed.

docs.title: Does Tank need ActiveMQ or another message queue?
docs.text: No. Older guides describe a JMS queue between the controller and agents. Current Tank uses HTTP and WebSocket only.

docs.title: Ideology: Gatling vs Tank
docs.text:
Gatling and Tank are both open-source load testing tools, but they start from different places.

Tank Gatling (open-source edition) How tests are written Recorded through the Tank Proxy, then cleaned up with filters and edited step by step in a web UI. Written as code in Gatling's DSL (Java, Scala or Kotlin), often starting from its recorder. Where tests live In the controller's database, shared by everyone who uses the controller. In source files, versioned with your code. Where load comes from Agents the controller starts on demand in AWS, in one or more regions. The machine that runs the simulation. Running and watching tests Queued and controlled from the web UI or the REST API, with live users, TPS and failures per job and per agent in the Agent Tracker. Run from the command line or a build tool, with an HTML report at the end. Test data Data files uploaded to the controller and split among agents. Feeders defined in the simulation code. Access control Users, groups and ownership (see Roles and permissions). None; anyone with the code can run it.

Tank suits teams that want a shared, central place to record, keep and run load tests at scale without writing code. Gatling suits teams that want load tests as code alongside their application.

docs.title: Roles and Permissions
docs.text:
Tank controls who can do what with groups. Each user belongs to one or more groups, and each group grants a set of rights. Administrators assign groups on the Admin › Users page.

Three rules apply on top of the groups:

  • Everyone who is signed in can view every project, script, filter, filter group and data file, and the Agent Tracker.
  • Owners can always change and delete what they own, and can queue, run and control the jobs of projects they own, whatever their groups.
  • Members of the admin group can do everything, including the administration pages.

The owner of an item is the user who created it. The owner or an administrator can give a project, filter or filter group to another user by changing its Owner.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
These are the groups in Tank's default configuration. New users, whether created by an administrator or signed in for the first time through SSO, get the default groups, user and guest.

Group Role guest Can view everything, but has no rights to create or change anything. (default) user Can create projects, scripts, filters and filter groups, and upload data files. Can only change and delete what they own. (default) project-manager Maintains projects: can create, change and delete anyone's projects, control any project's jobs, and upload and delete data files. Can't create scripts or filters. script-manager Maintains scripts and filters: can create, change and delete anyone's scripts, filters and filter groups, and upload and delete data files. Can't create projects or control jobs. job-manager Controls jobs: can run, pause, stop, kill and delete any project's jobs. Can't create or change projects. admin Can do everything.

docs.title: Rights
docs.text:
The rights, and the groups that hold them by default:

Right Lets you Default groups Create Project create and copy projects user, project-manager Edit Project change anyone's project project-manager Delete Project delete anyone's project project-manager Create Script create, copy and import scripts; create external filter scripts user, script-manager Edit Script change anyone's script, including applying filters to it script-manager Delete Script delete anyone's script script-manager Create Filter create and copy filters and filter groups user, script-manager Edit Filter change anyone's filter or filter group script-manager Delete Filter delete anyone's filter or filter group script-manager Create Data File upload data files user, script-manager, project-manager Edit Data File replace the contents of anyone's data file none (owners and admins only) Delete Data File delete anyone's data file script-manager, project-manager Control Job queue, run and control any project's jobs, and delete jobs that haven't started job-manager, project-manager

docs.title: Permissions matrix
docs.text:
What each default group can do with items it doesn't own. You can always change and delete items you own, and admins can do everything.

guest user project-manager script-manager job-manager Projects: view Projects: create Projects: change, delete Jobs: queue, run, control Scripts: view Scripts: create Scripts: change, delete Filters and groups: view Filters and groups: create Filters and groups: change, delete Data files: view Data files: upload Data files: replace contents Data files: delete

docs.title: Changing the groups and rights
docs.text:
The groups, the default groups and the rights each group holds are set in the security section of the controller's settings.xml:

<security>
    <groups>
        <group>admin</group>
        <group isDefault="true">user</group>
        <group>script-manager</group>
        <group>project-manager</group>
        <group>job-manager</group>
        <group isDefault="true">guest</group>
    </groups>
    <restrictions>
        <restriction operation="CREATE_PROJECT">
            <groups>
                <group>user</group>
                <group>project-manager</group>
            </groups>
        </restriction>
        <!-- one restriction per right: CREATE_, EDIT_ and DELETE_ PROJECT, SCRIPT,
             FILTER and DATAFILE, and CONTROL_JOB -->
    </restrictions>
</security>

isDefault="true" marks the groups new users get. A right with no restriction is held by no group, so only owners and admins have it.

REST security

These rules apply to the web UI and to REST calls when rest-security-enabled is true in settings.xml. When it is false, REST calls without credentials are allowed, as they were before REST authorization existed. Enable it on any shared controller.

docs.title: Supplemental Tools
docs.text:
Tank ships four tools that run on your own machine, alongside the controller:

Tool File What it does Agent Visual Debugger Tank-Debugger-all.jar Steps through a script request by request. With --headless, replays a project from the command line Script Filter Editor Tank-Script-Runner-all.jar Writes and tests external (JavaScript) filters against a Tank XML script Tank Proxy Tank-Proxy-pkg.zip Records a browser session as a Tank XML script to upload API Test Harness apiharness-1.0-all.jar The agent's harness, for running a harness XML file locally from the command line

All of them need Java 21 or later. Each one is built with the controller that serves it, so download them from the controller you use.

docs.title: From the web UI
docs.text:
Open the Tools page. It lists each tool with the controller's version and build date, and a download link for each.

Release builds only

The controller has the tools only when it was built with mvn clean install -P release. A development build has none: the download returns 404, and the Tools page in the new UI shows "Not included in this build".

docs.title: With an API token
docs.text:
Scripts and CI jobs can download each tool from the REST API with a user's API token, instead of a web login:

Tool Endpoint File Agent Visual Debugger GET /v2/tools/debugger Tank-Debugger-all.jar Script Filter Editor GET /v2/tools/script-runner Tank-Script-Runner-all.jar Tank Proxy GET /v2/tools/proxy Tank-Proxy-pkg.zip API Test Harness GET /v2/tools/api-harness apiharness-1.0-all.jar 
curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TANK_TOKEN" -o Tank-Debugger-all.jar <tank_url>/v2/tools/debugger
Status Meaning 200 The file 401 No user is signed in, or the token is invalid 403 The agent token was used. These endpoints need a user's token or session 404 The controller was built without -P release, so it has no tools

Create your API token on your account page in the web UI (see Authentication).

docs.title: Agent Visual Debugger
docs.text:
Tank-Debugger-all.jar runs a script on your machine one request at a time, showing each request, response and variable as it goes.

Start it by double-clicking the jar, or from the command line. On the command line you can give the controller URL, and optionally your API token, as positional arguments:

java -jar Tank-Debugger-all.jar                                  # pick the Tank instance later
java -jar Tank-Debugger-all.jar https://tank.example.com      # connect to this controller
java -jar Tank-Debugger-all.jar https://tank.example.com <token>

docs.title: Using the debugger
docs.text:
• Connect to a Tank: File > Select Tank Instance... asks for the base URL and your API token. It checks the connection before using it.
  • Load a script: open a file from disk, or use Choose Script or Choose Project to load one from the connected controller. Reload fetches it again. Choose Datafile and Show Project Variables supply the data a project's script uses.
  • Run: Start, Next Step, Skip, Run to Breakpoint..., Pause and Stop are on the toolbar, the Run menu and the script's right-click menu. Set breakpoints and skipped steps with Toggle Breakpoint and Toggle Skip Step on the right-click menu, and clear them all with Clear All Breakpoints and Clear All Skips.
  • HTTP client: pick which agent HTTP client runs the requests. The list comes from the connected controller.
  • Sleep and think steps: the Run Sleep Steps and Run Think Steps check boxes decide whether timing steps actually wait. Both are off by default.
  • Output: the Actions menu saves the requests and responses (debuggerOutput.txt) or the log (debuggerLog.txt), and clears the log output.

docs.title: debugger.properties
docs.text:
On first use the debugger writes debugger.properties to the directory you start it from. Edit it to list the controllers in the Select Tank Instance drop-down and to set the timing-step defaults:

# One line per controller: tank.instance.<name>=<base url>
tank.instance.TANK=http://tank-url

# Set to true to run sleep/think steps, false to skip them
run.sleep.steps=false
run.think.steps=false

When you connect to an instance from the list with a token, the debugger saves that token in the same file as tank.token.<name>. Keep the file private.

docs.title: Headless mode
docs.text:
With --headless, the same jar replays a Tank project from the command line, with no window. It is meant for Jenkins jobs and scripts. It writes the authid and the result of each step to files in the current directory.

java -jar Tank-Debugger-all.jar --headless -h=<controller_base_url> -p=<projectId> -t=<token>
Option Meaning --headless Run from the command line. Without it, the visual debugger opens -h, --host Tank controller URL, for example https://tank.example.com (required; include the context path, such as /tank, if the war isn't deployed as ROOT.war) -p, --project Id of the Tank project whose script to run (required) -t, --token Tank API token (required) --help Usage and exit codes --version Build version and git commit

The exit code reports whether the run finished. It does not validate the result: read output.log for that.

Code Meaning 0 The run finished 1 The script failed the hostname replacement check (not filtered for production) 2 Invalid command line arguments 3 Could not get the project or its script from Tank 4 The run could not be started or did not finish

Output files, written to the current working directory:

  • output.log: the result summary, one key,value per line. The line authid,<value> is the authid. Other lines: project, project_id, username, srsversion, total_steps, total_executed, execution_percentage, taxhub_flow, filing_status, timestamp. Failed steps also log the full request, response and variables.
  • validation-report.json: every step with its pass or fail result and validation errors.
  • debugger.log: general debug log.

The machine must reach the Tank controller over HTTP(S), and the hosts the replayed script calls.

docs.title: Script Filter Editor
docs.text:
Tank-Script-Runner-all.jar (window title "Intuit Tank Script Filter Editor") is for writing and testing external filters: scripts that change a Tank script's steps when an internal filter can't express the change.

java -jar Tank-Script-Runner-all.jar
java -jar Tank-Script-Runner-all.jar https://tank.example.com <token>

The optional positional arguments are the controller URL (default http://localhost:8080/) and your API token. The controller is only used in remote storage mode.

To test a filter:

  1. Select Tank XML > Select File... loads a script exported from Tank (GET /v2/scripts/download/{scriptId} returns this format).
  2. Choose the script language, write the filter in the editor, and click Run Script. The filter reads the loaded script with ioBean.getInput("script"), the same input the controller gives external filters when it applies them, and can log with ioBean.println, ioBean.debug and ioBean.error. Output appears in the lower pane.
  3. Show XML displays the script after the filter ran; Save XML writes it to a file.

Open Script..., Save Script... and Save Script As... work on the local disk in local storage mode (the default). Toggle Storage Mode switches to remote mode, where they list and save the controller's external scripts instead.

Languages

JavaScript (Nashorn) is always included. Groovy and Ruby (JRuby) appear in the language list only when the jar was built with mvn clean install -P release,script-engines.

docs.title: Tank Proxy (recorder)
docs.text:
The Tank Proxy records the traffic of a browser session and saves it as Tank XML, which you then upload as a new script (see Importing a recorded Script).

Tank-Proxy-pkg.zip unzips to an Intuit-Tank-Proxy directory containing:

File Purpose Tank-Proxy-all.jar The recording proxy startProxy.sh Runs java -jar Tank-Proxy-all.jar recording-proxy-config-default.xml Default settings: port 8888, output file outputFile.xml, and image and PDF response bodies excluded auto_generated_ca.p12, auto_generated_ca.pem The certificate authority the proxy signs HTTPS certificates with readme.txt Setup notes

Run it from that directory, so it finds the configuration and the CA files:

cd Intuit-Tank-Proxy
java -jar Tank-Proxy-all.jar

docs.title: Recording a session
docs.text:
1. Trust the proxy's CA in your browser or operating system: import auto_generated_ca.pem as a trusted certificate authority ("OWASP Custom CA for Tank"). On Windows you can import the .p12 from the command prompt with certutil -f -p password -importpfx auto_generated_ca.p12. If the .p12 is missing from the working directory, the proxy generates a new CA and writes a new auto_generated_ca.pem, which you must trust instead.
  2. Set your browser's HTTP and HTTPS proxy to localhost and the proxy port (8888 by default).
  3. Optionally open File > Settings to change the port, the output file and the request and body inclusion and exclusion rules. The settings dialog can save and open them as XML files.
  4. Click Start Recording (also in the Session menu). Pause Recording and Stop Recording are next to it.
  5. Exercise the application in the browser. Each transaction appears in the table; use the filter box to search them and Delete Selected to drop ones you don't want.
  6. Click Stop Recording, then Save (File menu). File > Open Recording... reopens a saved recording, and Session > Hosts... lists the hosts that were recorded.
  7. Upload the saved XML to Tank as a new script.

docs.title: API Test Harness
docs.text:
apiharness-1.0-all.jar is the harness the agents run. Locally it runs a harness XML file (which you can download with GET /v2/projects/download/{projectId} or GET /v2/scripts/harness/download/{scriptId}) from the command line, which helps when you debug a script:

java -jar apiharness-1.0-all.jar -tp=<test plan file> [options]
Option Meaning -tp=<file> The harness XML file to run. Several files can be given, separated by commas -users=<n> Number of users to run concurrently -start=<n> Number of users to start with -ramp=<minutes> Time to get from the start users to the full number of users -time=<minutes> Length of the simulation -d Debug: step through each request -t Trace: print each request

The harness's other options (-http, -token, -jobId and so on) are how a controller starts an agent, and are not needed for a local run.

docs.title: Jenkins plugin (not built)
docs.text: tools/jenkins_plugin holds the source of an old Jenkins plugin that started a Tank Proxy before a build and stopped it afterwards. It is not part of any build (its module is commented out in tools/pom.xml) and is not shipped. To run Tank from Jenkins, download the tools with an API token and use the debugger's headless mode or the REST API.

docs.title: Using the REST API
docs.text: The Tank controller has a JSON REST API, version 2, under /v2. The web UI uses it, and scripts and CI jobs can use it too. Every endpoint is listed in the API Reference.

docs.title: Base URL
docs.text:
Requests go to the controller's base URL followed by /v2/.... The installation guide deploys Tank as Tomcat's ROOT.war, so the base URL is the host, for example https://tank.example.com. If you deployed tank.war under its own name, add the context path: https://tank.example.com/tank. The examples below use $TANK for it.

TANK=https://tank.example.com
curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TANK_TOKEN" "$TANK/v2/ping"

Bodies are JSON unless an endpoint says otherwise. File downloads (scripts, harness XML, tools) and a few plain-text responses such as the ping endpoints are the exceptions; the reference shows each endpoint's media types.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: The API accepts two kinds of credentials.

docs.title: API token
docs.text:
Send a user's API token as a bearer token:

curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TANK_TOKEN" "$TANK/v2/me"

The request runs as that user, with that user's groups and rights. This is the method to use from scripts and CI.

Create the token in the web UI, on your account page (Account Settings in the classic UI), or call POST /v2/me/api-token from a signed-in session. Each user has one token: generating a new one replaces the old one, and the token is only shown when it is generated. DELETE /v2/me/api-token removes it.

An invalid token is never replaced by a session login: the request is treated as having no credentials (see Unauthenticated requests).

The agent token

Agents authenticate with the controller's agent token, also as Authorization: Bearer. It is meant for agents, not for people or scripts. Operations that act as a signed-in user, such as /v2/me and /v2/tools/..., refuse it with 403.

docs.title: Session login
docs.text:
The web UI logs in with a session cookie. You can do the same with curl:

# Log in: sets the session cookie and an XSRF-TOKEN cookie
curl -fsS -c cookies.txt -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username":"<user>","password":"<password>"}' \
  "$TANK/v2/auth/login"

# Read with the session
curl -fsS -b cookies.txt "$TANK/v2/me"

State-changing requests (anything but GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE) made with a session must send the value of the XSRF-TOKEN cookie in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header, or they are rejected with 403 "Missing or invalid CSRF token". Requests made with an API token don't need it.

XSRF=$(awk '$6 == "XSRF-TOKEN" {print $7}' cookies.txt)
curl -fsS -b cookies.txt -H "X-XSRF-TOKEN: $XSRF" -X POST "$TANK/v2/me/api-token"

POST /v2/auth/logout ends the session. When single sign-on is configured, the browser logs in through GET /v2/auth/sso/authorize instead; GET /v2/auth/config tells a client whether SSO is available.

docs.title: Unauthenticated requests
docs.text:
Only /v2/auth/config, /v2/auth/login, /v2/auth/sso/authorize and /v2/auth/sso/callback are always open.

Whether the rest of the API requires credentials depends on rest-security-enabled in the controller's settings.xml:

  • true: any other request without valid credentials gets 401.
  • false (the default in the shipped settings.xml): requests without credentials are allowed and run with full rights, except operations that need a signed-in user, such as /v2/me and /v2/tools/..., which still return 401.

With credentials, each endpoint checks the caller's rights (see Roles) and returns 403 when the caller lacks them.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors from the API's own checks have a JSON body (ErrorResponse in the reference):

{
  "message": "Resource not found: ...",
  "debugInfo": null
}
Field Meaning message What went wrong, for showing to a user debugInfo The stack trace when the server sets server.include-debug-info: true; otherwise null

The status code carries the kind of error: 400 for a bad request or parameter, 401 when not signed in, 403 when not allowed, 404 when not found, 409 for a conflict, and 500 for a server error. Authentication failures caught before a request reaches the API (a bad token, a missing CSRF token) have only message, for example {"message":"Unauthorized"}.

Framework errors return a plain-text message instead of JSON, for example Incorrect request body (400) when the body can't be read, File upload error: incorrect request or missing file parameter (400), or Not Found (404) for a path that doesn't exist.

docs.title: Paging
docs.text:
These list endpoints can return one page at a time:

Endpoint Default sort GET /v2/projects modified,desc GET /v2/scripts modified,desc GET /v2/datafiles modified,desc GET /v2/admin/users (always paged) name,asc Parameter Meaning page Zero-based page number. On projects, scripts and data files it selects the paged form: without it, the endpoint returns every item unpaged size Page size, 1 to 200 (default 25) sort A field name, optionally followed by ,asc or ,desc. The reference lists the fields each endpoint accepts q Text to search for (in the name, product or comments; for users, the name or email) owner Only items owned by this user (not on users)

A paged response looks like this:

{
  "items": [ ... ],
  "page": 0,
  "size": 25,
  "total": 132
}

An invalid page, size or sort returns 400.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
List the 10 most recently modified projects whose name, product or comments contain checkout:

curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TANK_TOKEN" \
  "$TANK/v2/projects?page=0&size=10&sort=modified,desc&q=checkout"

Get one project, then download its harness XML file:

curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TANK_TOKEN" "$TANK/v2/projects/42"
curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TANK_TOKEN" -OJ "$TANK/v2/projects/download/42"

Download the agent visual debugger built with this controller (see Supplemental Tools):

curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TANK_TOKEN" -o Tank-Debugger-all.jar "$TANK/v2/tools/debugger"

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
This page documents every endpoint of the Tank REST V2 API: its parameters, request and response bodies, and status codes. See Using the REST API for the base URL, authentication, errors and paging.

Generated from the code

The specification below is generated from the REST V2 controllers when this documentation is built, so it matches the code on master. A controller of a different version may differ.

A running controller serves its own specification: the Swagger UI at <tank_url>/swagger-ui.html and the OpenAPI JSON at <tank_url>/v3/api-docs, where <tank_url> is the controller's base URL, for example https://tank.example.com (add /tank if the war isn't deployed as ROOT.war). Use "Try it out" there, against that controller, rather than on this page.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The controller is configured by one XML file, settings.xml. This page lists every setting the code reads, with the value it uses when the setting is missing.

docs.title: Where the file lives
docs.text:
Tank looks for settings.xml in this order:

  1. settings.xml in the controller's working directory (for Tomcat, the directory you start it from).
  2. $WATS_PROPERTIES/settings.xml, where WATS_PROPERTIES is an environment variable or, if that isn't set, a Java system property (-DWATS_PROPERTIES=/path).

If the file doesn't exist, Tank writes its built-in default (api/src/main/resources/settings.xml in the source) to that location on first start, creating the folder if needed. Edit that copy, then restart the controller.

The root element is <tank-settings>. Each section below is independent and can appear in any order. Relative paths are resolved from the controller's working directory.

Settings for agents

Agents download the controller's settings file when they start, and the agent settings below are read from that copy. If a file named agent-settings.xml sits next to settings.xml, agents get it instead. Use it to keep credentials, SSO settings and other controller-only values off agent machines.

docs.title: Global settings
docs.text: Element Default Description instance-name prod The name of this controller, without spaces. Tank tags each agent instance with it (Controller tag) and uses the tag to find its own agents after a restart. Give every controller sharing an AWS account a different name. controller-base-url http://tank.controller/ The URL agents use to reach the controller. Include the context path if Tank isn't deployed at the root (for example http://host:8080/tank). Agents receive it in their EC2 user data. standalone false true means the controller doesn't start EC2 agents and uses registered standalone agents instead. See Standalone deployment. data-file-storage /tmp/tank/datafiles Where uploaded data files are stored. A local path, or an S3 bucket written as s3:bucket-name. jar-file-storage /tmp/tank/jars Files in this location are zipped and sent to every agent as support files, along with the test harness. A local path or s3:bucket-name. tmp-file-storage /tmp/tank/tmpfiles Scratch space for generated scripts and the support-file zip. Must be a local path. s3-encrypt false true to request server-side encryption when writing to S3 storage. rest-security-enabled false true rejects /v2 REST calls that carry no credentials (a session, a user API token or the agent token) with HTTP 401. When false, unauthenticated calls are allowed and permission checks pass for them. The login endpoints are always open. banner-text empty A notice shown to users in the web UI. user-auto-deletion-enabled false On startup, Tank looks for users who haven't logged in for the retention period. When false it only logs what it would do; when true it deletes (anonymizes) them. Can also be turned on with the system property tank.user.auto-deletion.enabled or the environment variable TANK_USER_AUTO_DELETION_ENABLED. user-auto-deletion-retention-days 730 The inactivity period for user auto-deletion. The system property tank.user.auto-deletion.retention-days overrides it. user-auto-deletion-permitted-users empty A comma-separated list of user names that auto-deletion never removes.

docs.title: Products and locations
docs.text:
Lists the users can pick from in the UI. They're labels only.

<products>
  <product name="">All Products</product>
  <product name="MyProduct">My Product</product>
</products>

<locations>
  <location name="unspecified" displayName="Unspecified" />
  <location name="san_diego" displayName="San Diego, CA" />
</locations>

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Chooses how agents report results and how the controller reads them back. Without this section Tank uses the database reporter.

<reporting>
  <provider>
    <reporter>com.intuit.tank.reporting.db.DatabaseResultsReporter</reporter>
    <reader>com.intuit.tank.reporting.db.DatabaseResultsReader</reader>
    <config></config>
  </provider>
</reporting>
Reporter / reader Use com.intuit.tank.reporting.db.DatabaseResultsReporter / ...DatabaseResultsReader The default. Writes results to the store set by vm-manager/results/provider (CloudWatch in the default file). com.intuit.tank.reporting.rest.RestResultsReporter / ...RestResultsReader Agents post results straight to the controller. Only for standalone or small tests: it overloads the controller under heavy load.

provider/config is passed to the reporter as-is.

docs.title: Agent settings: agent-config
docs.text:
Element Default Description agent-port 8090 The port agents listen on for the controller's HTTP and WebSocket calls. Open it from the controller to the agents. agent-token empty A shared secret that agents send as Authorization: Bearer <token>. A request with this token can do anything, so keep it secret. Set it when rest-security-enabled is true, and for standalone agents. agent-data-file-storage /tmp Where agents store data files during a test. connection-timeout 40000 HTTP connection timeout for test requests, in milliseconds. max-body-report-size 5000 The most response-body characters logged for a failed request. valid-mime-types/mime-type-regex none Regular expressions for the content types whose bodies are logged on error. The default file lists .*text.*, .*json.* and .*xml.*. log-post-response false true logs the response to each POST request. max-response-time 5000 If a response takes longer than this (ms), the agent waits extra time before the user's next request. max-failed-wait-time 180000 The longest extra wait after a slow response (ms). Helps keep a struggling server from backing up. over-simulation-max-time 7200000 How long a test may run past its planned simulation time (ms). status_report_interval_milis set by the caller How often agents report status (ms). The default file sets 30000. tps-period 15 The period, in seconds, over which agents calculate transactions per second. The default file sets 30. duration-simulation/simulation post 500–1000, get 50–300, process 10–50 Assumed request times (ms), by step type, used to estimate how long a script takes: <simulation for="get" min="50" max="300" />. request-headers/header none Headers added to every request: <header key="name">value</header>. tank-http-clients/tank-client Apache HttpClient 4.5, Apache HttpClient 5, JDK client The HTTP clients users can choose for a test: <tank-client name="Display name">class</tank-client>. default-tank-client Apache HttpClient 4.5 The display name of the default client. The default file sets JDK HttpClient. command-ws-enabled false true makes the controller send agent commands over a WebSocket connection to agent-port instead of plain HTTP calls. agent-readoption-enabled 0 Seconds between passes in which the controller reconnects to running agents found by their Controller and JobId tags, for example after a controller restart. 0 turns it off; the default file suggests 300. Needs command-ws-enabled; ignored in standalone mode.

The HTTP client classes that ship with Tank are:

Class Client com.intuit.tank.httpclient4.TankHttpClient4 Apache HttpClient 4.5 com.intuit.tank.httpclient5.TankHttpClient5 Apache HttpClient 5 com.intuit.tank.httpclientjdk.TankHttpClientJDK The JDK's java.net.http client

docs.title: Cloud settings: vm-manager
docs.text:
Element Default Description default-region US_EAST The default region for tests (a name from the region table below). use-agent-elastic-ips false Default for binding available Elastic IPs to agents. reserved-elastic-ips/eip none Elastic IPs that Tank must never bind to agents. tags/tag none Extra tags for agent instances: <tag name="admin_contact">tank_admin</tag>. Tank adds Name, Controller, JobId and JobName itself.

Regions use these names:

Name AWS region US_EAST us-east-1 US_EAST_2 us-east-2 US_WEST_1 us-west-1 US_WEST_2 us-west-2 EUROPE eu-west-1 ASIA_1 ap-southeast-1 ASIA_2 ap-southeast-2 ASIA_3 ap-northeast-1 SOUTH_AMERICA sa-east-1

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
<credentials type="amazon">
  <!-- <secret-key-id>...</secret-key-id> <secret-key>...</secret-key> -->
  <!-- <proxy-host></proxy-host> <proxy-port>80</proxy-port> -->
</credentials>

Keep this element, even empty: the controller expects it when it launches agents. With no keys, Tank uses the AWS SDK's default credential chain (an instance profile on EC2), which is the recommended setup.

Element Description secret-key-id-property The name of a Java system property or environment variable that holds the access key ID. Defaults to AWS_SECRET_KEY_ID. secret-key-property The same for the secret access key. Defaults to AWS_SECRET_KEY. secret-key-id, secret-key Keys written into the file, used only when the property or variable above is empty. proxy-host, proxy-port A proxy for the controller's EC2 API calls.

Warning

If access keys are configured by any of these means, the controller passes them to every agent in the EC2 user data.

docs.title: Instance descriptions
docs.text:
Each region you can run agents in needs an instance-descriptions block with an AGENT description. Only regions with one appear in the UI. Values in default-instance-description apply to every region unless the region sets its own.

<default-instance-description>
  <security-group>security_group</security-group>
  <keypair>myKey</keypair>
</default-instance-description>

<instance-descriptions region="US_WEST_2">
  <instance-description name="AGENT">
    <ami>[AMI-ID]</ami>
    <keypair>[KEYPAIR]</keypair>
    <iam-role>[INSTANCE-PROFILE-NAME]</iam-role>
    <vpc-subnet>[SUBNET-1]</vpc-subnet>
    <vpc-subnet>[SUBNET-2]</vpc-subnet>
    <security-group-ids>[SG-ID]</security-group-ids>
  </instance-description>
</instance-descriptions>
Element Description ami The agent AMI ID. ssm-ami The name of an SSM parameter holding the AMI ID. Used in preference to ami, which is the fallback if the lookup fails. The controller needs ssm:GetParameter. keypair The EC2 key pair name. iam-role The instance profile name to launch agents with. Recommended over access keys. vpc-subnet A subnet to launch agents in. Repeat it to spread agents over several subnets. security-group-ids Security group IDs for agents in a VPC. security-group A security group name, used when security-group-ids is empty. zone An Availability Zone to place agents in. Tenancy EC2 tenancy (for example dedicated). Defaults to default. Note the capital T. vpc true if Elastic IPs for these agents are VPC addresses. public-ip An Elastic IP to bind when a single agent is launched.

Note

The element is instance-description. Older copies of the settings file, including assets/settings-all-in-one.xml, spell it instance-descripion; Tank ignores that spelling.

docs.title: Instance types
docs.text:
The agent sizes users can choose, and the figures Tank uses to estimate cost and agent count:

<instance-types type="amazon">
  <type name="m.xlarge" types="m8g.xlarge,m7g.xlarge" cost=".1795" users="2000"
        cpus="4" ecus="16" mem="16" default="true"
        jvmArgs="-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=70.0 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70.0 -XX:+UseG1GC" />
</instance-types>
Attribute Description name The name shown to users. types Required. A comma-separated list of EC2 instance types for this size. cost Hourly cost, for estimates. users Users one agent of this size runs. cpus, ecus, mem Informational sizes. jvmArgs JVM options for the agent's test harness. default true for the size selected by default.

The default file's sizes are Graviton (arm64) types, so the agent AMI must be arm64.

docs.title: Watchdog
docs.text:
The watchdog checks that launched agents report in, and relaunches them if they don't. Durations are written like 30s, 3m or 1h.

Element Default Description watchdog/max-time-for-agent-report 3m How long to wait for agents to report before relaunching them. watchdog/max-time-for-agent-report-<region> the value above The same for one region, named by its AWS code, for example max-time-for-agent-report-us-east-2. watchdog/max-restarts 3 Relaunch attempts before the job is stopped. watchdog/sleep-time-between-check 30s How often the watchdog checks.

docs.title: Results store
docs.text:
Where DatabaseResultsReporter writes results:

<results>
  <provider>com.intuit.tank.persistence.databases.CloudWatchDataSource</provider>
  <config></config>
</results>

If provider is missing, Tank uses AmazonDynamoDatabaseDocApi; the default file sets CloudWatchDataSource.

Provider class (com.intuit.tank.persistence.databases.) Keys in results/config CloudWatchDataSource None. Writes metrics to the Intuit/Tank namespace. AmazonDynamoDatabaseDocApi read-capacity (default 10), write-capacity (default 50). S3Datasource bucket (default tank-test), metricString (default test.tank.transaction), tags. WavefrontDatasource wavefrontHost, wavefrontPort, metricString. GraphiteDatasource graphiteHost, graphitePort.

docs.title: Agent metrics
docs.text:
The controller reads agent CPU, memory, JVM and TCP metrics from CloudWatch for the Agent Tracker. Agents must publish them (see the CloudWatch agent setup in aws-config/tank_agent.yml).

Element Default Description agent-metrics/enabled true Turns collection on or off. agent-metrics/poll-interval-seconds 60 How often to poll CloudWatch. Minimum 15. agent-metrics/retention-points 60 Data points kept per agent. Minimum 2. agent-metrics/finished-job-grace-minutes 15 How long to keep collecting after a job finishes. agent-metrics/vcpus 0 The agents' vCPU count. CloudWatch reports CPU as a percentage of one core; with this set, Tank divides by it. 0 caps the figure at 100 instead.

docs.title: Security: security
docs.text:
Defines groups, which groups can do what, and users created on startup. See Roles and permissions for what the groups mean.

<security>
  <groups>
    <group>admin</group>
    <group isDefault="true">user</group>
    <group>script-manager</group>
    <group>project-manager</group>
    <group>job-manager</group>
    <group isDefault="true">guest</group>
  </groups>
  <restrictions>
    <restriction operation="CREATE_PROJECT">
      <groups>
        <group>user</group>
        <group>project-manager</group>
      </groups>
    </restriction>
    <!-- ... -->
  </restrictions>
  <users>
    <user>
      <name>admin</name>
      <password>admin</password>
      <email>admin@example.com</email>
      <group>admin</group>
    </user>
  </users>
</security>
Element Description groups/group The groups that exist. Tank creates any that are missing on startup. isDefault="true" groups are given to new users. restrictions/restriction For each operation, the groups allowed to perform it. The default file covers CREATE_PROJECT, DELETE_PROJECT, EDIT_PROJECT, CREATE_SCRIPT, DELETE_SCRIPT, EDIT_SCRIPT, CREATE_FILTER, DELETE_FILTER, EDIT_FILTER, CREATE_DATAFILE, DELETE_DATAFILE and CONTROL_JOB. Admins can do everything. users/user Users created on startup if no user with that name exists, with password, email and one or more group entries (plus the default groups). Existing users are never changed, so editing the password here after the first start has no effect.

docs.title: Single sign-on: oidc-sso
docs.text:
Add this section to let users sign in through an OpenID Connect provider. If it's absent, SSO is off.

<oidc-sso>
  <client-id>...</client-id>
  <client-secret>/path/to/ssm/parameter</client-secret>
  <authorization-url>https://idp.example.com/oauth2/authorize</authorization-url>
  <redirect-url>https://tank.example.com/v2/auth/sso/callback</redirect-url>
  <issuer>idp.example.com</issuer>
  <token-endpoint>/oauth2/token</token-endpoint>
</oidc-sso>
Element Description client-id The client ID registered with the provider. The ID token's audience must match it. client-secret The client secret, or, if it starts with /, the name of an SSM SecureString parameter that holds it. authorization-url The provider's authorization URL users are sent to. redirect-url The callback URL registered with the provider. The REST API's callback, <controller-url>/v2/auth/sso/callback, completes the login and returns the user to the page that started it. issuer The provider's host name. Tank calls https://<issuer><token-endpoint> to exchange the code. token-endpoint The path of the token endpoint on that host.

OidcSsoConfig also defines authorization-endpoint, but nothing reads it.

docs.title: Script functions: logic-step
docs.text: logic-step/insert-before and logic-step/append-after hold JavaScript that Tank adds before and after every logic step script. The default file defines helper functions such as log, getVariable, setVariable, getResponseBody, gotoGroup and abortScript. Leave them unless you're adding helpers of your own.

docs.title: Settings with no effect
docs.text:
The default file and older guides contain these elements, but current code doesn't read them. You can delete them.

Element Note agent-config/agent-http-port The port setting is agent-port. agent-config/ssl-timeout Not read. agent-config/log-post-request, agent-config/log-variables Not read. timing-file-storage Not read. vm-manager/watchdog/max-time-for-agent-start Not read; only max-time-for-agent-report is used. vm-manager/default-instance-description/reuse-instances Not read. vm-manager/results/write-capacity Not read. DynamoDB capacity is set in results/config. mail Not read. No current code sends email.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page covers a production-style install in AWS: the AWS resources, the controller on Tomcat, and the agent image the controller launches. To try Tank on one machine first, see the Quickstart. Every setting mentioned here is described in Configuration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Component Version Java 21 or later. The build targets Java 21 (maven.compiler.release); the project badge lists 21 and 25. Apache Tomcat 11.0 (the build compiles against Tomcat 11.0.x). The project badge also lists 10.1. MySQL 8.x. The CloudFormation template creates RDS MySQL 8.4. The war bundles MySQL Connector/J (com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver). Maven Only to build from source. The build downloads its own Node.js to build the React UI.

docs.title: Choosing a JDK
docs.text:
Use an OpenJDK distribution approved by your organization, on both the controller and the agents, at the Java major version above. Don't select a JDK by version alone: point JAVA_HOME at the exact installation you intend to use.

macOSLinux 
# List installed JDKs and their paths
/usr/libexec/java_home -V

# Set JAVA_HOME to the exact JDK you chose
export JAVA_HOME=<path-to-intended-jdk>/Contents/Home
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"

export JAVA_HOME=<path-to-intended-jdk>
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"

Replace <path-to-intended-jdk> with the install directory of the JDK you chose. Then check it with java -version: the first line shows the major version (it must be 21 or later) and the runtime line names the vendor's build. Confirm both are what you intended before you build or deploy.

docs.title: Build Tank
docs.text:
export MAVEN_OPTS="$MAVEN_OPTS -Xms2g -Xmx3g"
mvn clean install -P release

The release profile also builds the agent packages and tools. A plain mvn clean install builds the war but not the agent zips.

Artifact Path Used for Controller web/web_ui/target/tank.war Deploy to Tomcat. Agent startup package agent/agent_startup_pkg/target/agent-startup-pkg.zip Baked into the agent AMI. Standalone agent package agent/agent_standalone_pkg/target/agent-standalone-pkg.zip Standalone agents. Debugger, script filter, proxy See Supplemental tools. Desktop tools.

docs.title: AWS resources
docs.text:
Tank uses these AWS services:

  • EC2: agent instances, AMIs, security groups, key pairs and, optionally, Elastic IPs bound to agents so the system under test can allow-list them.
  • RDS for MySQL (or any MySQL 8 server you run and back up yourself).
  • IAM: instance profiles for the controller and the agents.
  • CloudWatch: test results (the default results store), agent logs and host metrics.
  • S3: optional storage for data files and agent support files, and optional results storage.
  • SSM Parameter Store: optional, for the agent AMI ID and the OIDC client secret.
  • X-Ray: optional tracing of the controller.

The aws-config/ folder in the repository has CloudFormation templates for most of this:

Template Creates tank_instanceProfiles.yml The controller and agent IAM roles and instance profiles. It exports TankControllerProfile, which the controller template imports. Deploy it first. tank_controller.yml An RDS MySQL 8.4 instance, security groups, and a Graviton (arm64) Amazon Linux 2023 controller with Tomcat 11, the CloudWatch agent and the AWS OpenTelemetry Java agent. It takes the S3 locations of tank.war and settings.xml as parameters. tank_agent.yml A Graviton (arm64) Amazon Linux 2023 instance with the agent installed as a systemd service, ready to snapshot into an agent AMI. It takes the S3 location of agent-startup-pkg.zip.

Review the controller template before you use it

tank_controller.yml copies settings.xml to /usr/share/tomcat/settings.xml and the war to /usr/share/tomcat/webapps/ROOT.war, but it runs Tomcat from /opt/tomcat (working directory /opt/tomcat) and doesn't set WATS_PROPERTIES. As written, Tomcat won't find either file. Change those paths, or set WATS_PROPERTIES, before you rely on it. The templates also install Amazon Corretto 25 (java-25-amazon-corretto-headless); change the package if your organization requires a different OpenJDK distribution.

docs.title: Key pair
docs.text: Create an EC2 key pair in each region you will run agents in, and keep the private key: AWS can't give it back to you. The key pair name goes in the keypair setting.

docs.title: Security groups
docs.text:
Group Inbound rules Controller TCP 8080 (Tomcat) from your users and from the agents; SSH 22 from your admin network. Agents The agent port, TCP 8090 by default (agent-port), from the controller. The controller calls agents over HTTP and WebSocket on this port. Database TCP 3306 from the controller.

Agents also need outbound access to the controller's controller-base-url and to the systems under test.

docs.title: IAM
docs.text:
Prefer instance profiles to access keys. Without keys in settings.xml, Tank uses the AWS SDK's default credential chain, which picks up the instance profile.

tank_instanceProfiles.yml grants:

  • Controller role: the managed policies AmazonEC2FullAccess, AmazonS3FullAccess, AWSXrayWriteOnlyAccess and CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy, plus iam:PassRole, iam:ListInstanceProfiles, iam:AddRoleToInstanceProfile, appconfig:GetConfiguration, cloudwatch:GetMetricData and cloudwatch:ListMetrics. The controller needs iam:PassRole to launch agents with the agent instance profile, and cloudwatch:GetMetricData to show agent metrics.
  • Agent role: AmazonS3FullAccess and CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy, plus cloudwatch:PutMetricData and cloudwatch:PutMetricStream.

Note

The template's controller role has no ssm:GetParameter permission. Add it if you use ssm-ami for the agent AMI or an SSM parameter for the OIDC client secret. You can also narrow the managed policies to the buckets and actions you use.

If you can't use instance profiles, set access keys through the credentials element (see Configuration). The controller passes those keys to every agent in the EC2 user data.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: Create an empty database for Tank (the templates name it tank) and a user that can create and alter tables in it. Hibernate creates and updates the schema when the controller starts. Back the database up: it holds all your projects and scripts.

docs.title: Agent AMI
docs.text:
Agents run from an AMI you build once per region. The default instance types in settings.xml are Graviton (m7g, m8g), so build an arm64 AMI unless you change the instance types.

CloudFormationManual
  1. Upload agent-startup-pkg.zip to S3.
  2. Create a stack from aws-config/tank_agent.yml, passing the zip's S3 location as TankZip, a key pair, subnets and security groups.
  3. When the stack completes, create an AMI from the instance, then delete the stack.

On an arm64 Linux instance:

  1. Install an approved OpenJDK (Java 21 or later) and unzip.

  2. Unzip the package into /opt, which creates /opt/tank_agent, and create its log folder:

    sudo unzip agent-startup-pkg.zip -d /opt
sudo mkdir /opt/tank_agent/logs

  3. Start /opt/tank_agent/run.sh at boot from /opt/tank_agent. The template's unit file:

    [Unit]
Description=Tank agent
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
WorkingDirectory=/opt/tank_agent
ExecStart=/opt/tank_agent/run.sh
LimitNOFILE=20000
UMask=0077

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

  4. Raise the open-file limits and the ephemeral port range for high connection counts. The template sets DefaultLimitNOFILE=81960 for systemd and adds net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range=1024 65000 to /etc/sysctl.conf.

  5. Optionally install the CloudWatch agent to ship /opt/tank_agent/logs/agent.log and host metrics (see the template for the configuration).
  6. Create an AMI from the instance.

Put the AMI ID in the ami setting of each region's instance-description, or publish it as an SSM parameter and use ssm-ami.

When a test starts, the controller launches instances from this AMI with the controller URL, agent token and job details in the user data. The agent fetches its settings and support files from the controller and then starts the test harness.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
CloudFormationManual
  1. Deploy tank_instanceProfiles.yml.
  2. Upload tank.war and your settings.xml to S3.
  3. Deploy tank_controller.yml with those S3 locations, a VPC, subnets, a key pair and an RDS password. Read the warning under AWS resources first.
  1. Install an approved OpenJDK (Java 21 or later) and set JAVA_HOME as above.
  2. Download Tomcat 11 from tomcat.apache.org and unpack it, for example to /opt/tomcat.

  3. Remove the default applications and deploy Tank at the root context:

    rm -rf /opt/tomcat/webapps/*
cp web/web_ui/target/tank.war /opt/tomcat/webapps/ROOT.war

  4. Define the jdbc/watsDS data source in /opt/tomcat/conf/context.xml. This is the definition the controller template uses:

    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<Context>
    <Resource name="jdbc/watsDS" auth="Container"
        type="javax.sql.DataSource"
        factory="org.apache.tomcat.jdbc.pool.DataSourceFactory"
        maxWait="10000"
        username="admin" password="REPLACE_ME"
        testOnBorrow="true"
        validationQuery="SELECT 1"
        removeAbandonedOnBorrow="true"
        removeAbandonedOnMaintenance="true"
        removeAbandonedTimeout="60"
        driverClassName="com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver"
        url="jdbc:mysql://DB_HOST:3306/tank"/>
</Context>

  5. Tell Tank where its settings file lives. Tank reads settings.xml from Tomcat's working directory, or from the folder in the WATS_PROPERTIES environment variable or Java system property when the working directory has none. For example, in /opt/tomcat/bin/setenv.sh:

    export WATS_PROPERTIES=/opt/tank/conf

  6. Start Tomcat. If no settings file exists, Tank writes the default one to that location. Stop Tomcat, edit the file (at least controller-base-url, instance-name, the agent AMIs, the subnets and security groups, and the default admin password), and start Tomcat again.

Then open http://<controller-host>:8080/ and sign in. On first start Tank creates the users listed under security/users in settings.xml; the default file creates admin with the password admin. Change that password straight away, or change the entry before the first start.

Keep secrets away from agents

Agents download the controller's settings.xml. If a file named agent-settings.xml exists in the same folder, agents get that file instead, so you can keep credentials and SSO settings out of what agents receive.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Build the new war, replace ROOT.war and restart Tomcat. Tank updates the database schema on startup.

Agents keep running while the controller restarts. With command-ws-enabled set to true and agent-readoption-enabled set to a number of seconds, the restarted controller finds running agents by their Controller and JobId EC2 tags and reconnects to them.

docs.title: Standalone deployment
docs.text:
In standalone mode the controller doesn't start EC2 instances. Instead, standalone agents that you run yourself register with the controller and wait for work. Use it for small tests or where you can't use EC2.

  1. Install the controller and database as above.

  2. In settings.xml, set <standalone>true</standalone>. For small tests you can also send results straight to the controller with the REST reporter, as the all-in-one settings file (assets/settings-all-in-one.xml) does:

    <reporting>
  <provider>
    <reporter>com.intuit.tank.reporting.rest.RestResultsReporter</reporter>
    <reader>com.intuit.tank.reporting.rest.RestResultsReader</reader>
  </provider>
</reporting>

    The REST reporter sends every result through the controller, so don't use it for large tests.

  3. Set an agent-token in settings.xml. Standalone agents need a token to start.

  4. On each agent machine, unzip agent-standalone-pkg.zip and start the agent:

    java -jar agent-standalone-all.jar \
  -controller=http://<controller-host>:8080 \
  -token=<agent-token> \
  -host=<this-machine's-address> \
  -capacity=4000
    Option Meaning -controller Required. The controller's base URL. -token Required. The agent-token from settings.xml, or a user API token. -host The address the controller uses to reach this agent. Optional if the agent can work it out. -capacity The number of users this agent can run. Defaults to 4000.

The agent listens on TCP 1090 for the controller, so open that port to the controller. It reports its availability every five minutes. When it gets a job, it downloads the settings and support files into /opt/tank_agent (create that folder and make it writable by the agent's user) and runs ./startAgent.sh from its working directory.

When you start a test, the controller picks available standalone agents with enough total capacity for the test's users. If there isn't enough capacity, the job is aborted.

Standalone package not verified end to end

The run.sh and README.txt in the standalone package predate the required -token option, so run.sh as shipped exits with a usage message. The package also ships start_wats.sh rather than the startAgent.sh that the agent runs. Check both before you rely on standalone agents.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This page gets a Tank controller running on your own machine, with MySQL in Docker, so you can explore the UI, record and edit scripts, and build projects. It's for trying Tank out, not for large or production tests. For a full install, see Installation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• An OpenJDK distribution approved by your organization, Java 21 or later. Set JAVA_HOME to it explicitly and check it with java -version, as described in Choosing a JDK.
  • Maven, to build Tank.
  • Docker, for MySQL.
  • Apache Tomcat 11.

docs.title: 1. Build the war
docs.text:
From the root of the repository:

export MAVEN_OPTS="$MAVEN_OPTS -Xms2g -Xmx3g"
mvn clean install -DskipTests

The controller is web/web_ui/target/tank.war. Add -P release if you also want the agent packages and tools.

docs.title: 2. Start MySQL
docs.text:
docker run -d --name tank-mysql -p 3306:3306 \
  -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=tank \
  -e MYSQL_DATABASE=tank \
  -e MYSQL_USER=tank \
  -e MYSQL_PASSWORD=tank \
  mysql:8.4

You don't need to load a schema: Tank creates its tables when it starts.

docs.title: 3. Install Tomcat and Tank
docs.text:
Unpack Tomcat 11 somewhere, for example ~/tank/tomcat, then deploy Tank at the root context:

cd ~/tank/tomcat
rm -rf webapps/*
cp /path/to/Tank/web/web_ui/target/tank.war webapps/ROOT.war

Replace conf/context.xml with a data source for the database:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<Context>
    <Resource name="jdbc/watsDS" auth="Container"
        type="javax.sql.DataSource"
        factory="org.apache.tomcat.jdbc.pool.DataSourceFactory"
        maxWait="10000"
        username="tank" password="tank"
        testOnBorrow="true"
        validationQuery="SELECT 1"
        driverClassName="com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver"
        url="jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/tank"/>
</Context>

Tell Tank where to keep its settings file by creating bin/setenv.sh:

export WATS_PROPERTIES="$HOME/tank/conf"

docs.title: 4. Start, then configure
docs.text:
bin/catalina.sh run

On first start Tank writes a default settings.xml to ~/tank/conf, creates its tables, and creates the user admin with the password admin. Stop Tomcat (Ctrl+C) and edit ~/tank/conf/settings.xml for local use:

<controller-base-url>http://localhost:8080</controller-base-url>
<standalone>true</standalone>

Inside <agent-config>, set a token for agents:

<agent-token>choose-a-long-random-string</agent-token>

Inside <vm-manager>, turn off CloudWatch agent metrics, which need AWS credentials:

<agent-metrics>
  <enabled>false</enabled>
</agent-metrics>

Then replace the <reporting> section so results go straight to the controller instead of CloudWatch:

<reporting>
  <provider>
    <reporter>com.intuit.tank.reporting.rest.RestResultsReporter</reporter>
    <reader>com.intuit.tank.reporting.rest.RestResultsReader</reader>
  </provider>
</reporting>

Start Tomcat again and open:

  • http://localhost:8080/: the web UI. Sign in as admin / admin, then change the password.
  • http://localhost:8080/classic/: the classic JSF UI.

See Configuration for everything else in the file.

docs.title: 5. Run a test
docs.text:
In standalone mode the controller doesn't start agents in AWS: it uses standalone agents that register with it. See Standalone deployment for how to start one, and read the warning there first.

To check a script or project without any agents, use the Tank debugger (Tank-Debugger-all.jar, built by -P release). See Supplemental tools.

To run tests from EC2 agents instead, set <standalone>false</standalone>, give the controller AWS credentials, and complete the agent setup in Installation.

docs.title: Older quickstart scripts
docs.text:
The repository has two older quickstart paths. Neither works as shipped with current Tank:

all-in-one.sh

The script downloads Tank 4.2.0 artifacts, not the current release. It fetches the settings file from a GitHub page URL (.../blob/...), which returns HTML rather than XML. The context.xml it writes starts with a #!/bin/bash line before the XML declaration. Its start.sh sets -XX:PermSize and -XX:MaxPermSize, which current JVMs reject at startup. Its generated agent run.sh loses the controller URL, host and capacity values (they're expanded while the script runs) and passes no -token.

docker-experimental/

The Compose file starts MySQL 5.7; Tank's deployment template uses MySQL 8.4. setup.sh copies a schema into a container named docker_db_1, which only matches if you run Compose from a folder named docker, and the schema dump is years older than the current data model. The bundled context.xml and MySQL driver are for Tomcat 8.5. Hibernate creates the tables itself, so you don't need the schema; use the steps above instead.

docs.title: Data Files
docs.text: Data files feed your scripts with test data, such as logins, account numbers or search terms, so each virtual user works with different values. A project lists the data files its scripts read, and when a job runs, each file's lines are divided evenly among the job's agents.

docs.title: The Data files page
docs.text:
Open Data files in the menu bar. Like the other lists, it is paged, searchable, can be narrowed to one owner, and remembers your columns.

Each row can be:

  • previewed, 50 lines a page;
  • downloaded;
  • given new contents (Replace contents): upload a .csv, .txt or .xml file, or a gzipped .gz one. The data file keeps its name, so projects that use it get the new contents in their next job;
  • deleted. Tick several rows to delete them together.

docs.title: Uploading data files
docs.text:
1. Click Upload (or Upload data files on a project's Data files tab, which also adds the files to the project).
  2. Choose .csv, .txt or .xml files, or .zip files. Every .csv, .txt and .xml file in a zip, in any folder, becomes a data file named after it. You can upload up to 50 files at once.
  3. Click Upload.

A name that is already in use adds another file with that name; it doesn't replace the existing one. Use Replace contents to update a file.

You need the Create Data File right to upload. Replacing or deleting someone else's file needs Edit Data File or Delete Data File; you can always replace and delete your own. See Roles and permissions.

docs.title: Reading data in a script
docs.text:
Scripts read data files with the ioFunctions functions:

  • #{ioFunctions.getCSVData(column)} reads the default data file: the job's only data file, when it has exactly one.
  • #{ioFunctions.getCSVData('fileName', column)} reads a named file, for when a project has several, such as one for personal details and one for login credentials.

Columns are numbered from 0. Each virtual user works through its own lines, and no two users on an agent get the same line. IO Functions explains how lines are handed out and what happens when a file runs out.

Tip

Add every data file your scripts read to the project. A job only sends its agents the project's data files.

docs.title: How lines are divided among agents
docs.text: When a job starts, the controller divides each data file's lines evenly among the job's agents, so each agent reads a different part of the file. With 6,000 lines and two agents, each agent gets 3,000 lines. When the lines don't divide evenly, the few left over aren't used.

docs.title: Date Functions
docs.text:
dateFunctions return the current date and time as strings. A format is a Java date pattern such as yyyy-MM-dd or MM/dd/yyyy HH:mm:ss (SimpleDateFormat syntax). An empty or invalid format falls back to the agent locale's default date format, unless the row says otherwise.

Function Description Example currentDate(format) Today's date in the agent's time zone. #{dateFunctions.currentDate('yyyy-MM-dd')} returns 2011-11-15 on November 15, 2011 currentDate(format, timeZone) Today's date in timeZone, such as 'PST', 'America/Los_Angeles' or 'GMT'. A blank timeZone uses the agent's. #{dateFunctions.currentDate('yyyy-MM-dd', 'America/Los_Angeles')} currentDateTime(format) The current date and time in the agent's time zone. An empty format gives yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss. #{dateFunctions.currentDateTime('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss')} returns e.g. 2025-08-18 22:11:28 currentDateTime(format, timeZone) The current date and time in timeZone. #{dateFunctions.currentDateTime('HH:mm', 'GMT')} currentUTC() The current UTC time in ISO 8601 format. #{dateFunctions.currentUTC()} returns e.g. 2025-08-18T22:11:28.600Z currentUTC(format) The current UTC time in format, or one of the named formats below. An empty or invalid format gives ISO 8601. #{dateFunctions.currentUTC('ISO_UTC_NO_MS')} returns e.g. 2025-08-18T22:11:28Z addDays(days, format) The date days days from today in the agent's time zone. Use a negative days to go back. #{dateFunctions.addDays(5, 'yyyy-MM-dd')} returns 2011-11-20 on November 15, 2011 currentTimeMilis() Milliseconds since the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970 UTC). Note the spelling: one l. #{dateFunctions.currentTimeMilis()} returns e.g. 1357842009812

docs.title: Named UTC formats
docs.text:
currentUTC (and the legacy #function.date.currentUTC and #function.date.addDaysUTC) accept these names in place of a pattern:

Name Pattern Example ISO_UTC yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z' 2025-08-18T22:11:28.600Z ISO_UTC_NO_MS yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss'Z' 2025-08-18T22:11:28Z ISO_UTC_OFFSET yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSSXXX 2025-08-18T22:11:28.600Z ISO_UTC_DATE yyyy-MM-dd 2025-08-18 ISO_UTC_TIME HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z' 22:11:28.600Z RFC_1123 EEE, dd MMM yyyy HH:mm:ss zzz Mon, 18 Aug 2025 22:11:28 Z

No addDaysUTC in #{...}

There is no dateFunctions.addDaysUTC; #{dateFunctions.addDaysUTC(...)} returns an empty string. To add days in UTC, use the legacy form #function.date.addDaysUTC.<days>.<format>, for example #function.date.addDaysUTC.1.ISO_UTC. See Legacy #function syntax.

docs.title: Filters and Filter Groups
docs.text:
A recording captures everything the browser did, including analytics calls, static files and values that only made sense once. Filters clean up and enhance a recorded script so it behaves more like a real user: they can remove requests, rewrite hosts and headers, add think times, validations and assignments, and more.

A filter group is a named set of filters to apply together, such as every filter for one product or environment.

Filters run when you:

  • create a script from a recording, by ticking filters or groups under Filters to apply (see Importing a recorded script); ticking a group ticks all its filters, and you can untick the ones you don't need;
  • click Apply filters in the script editor, which changes the open script without saving it.

Filters run in the order of the filter list.

docs.title: The Filters page
docs.text:
Open Filters in the menu bar. The page has two tables, Filter groups and Filters. Each can be searched by name or ID, narrowed to a product, and sorted.

  • In the groups table, the count in a group's Filters column shows that group's filters in the filters table. The filters table can also be narrowed to one group.
  • Each row can be opened, copied under a new name, or deleted. Tick several rows to delete them together.
  • External filters opens the list of external scripts (see below).

docs.title: Creating a filter
docs.text:
1. Click New filter.
  2. Enter a Name, and optionally choose a Product.
  3. Choose the Filter type: Internal (rules you build here) or External (a script).
  4. Build the rules, or choose the external script, and click Create.

As in the other editors, Save, Revert and Save as… work on the whole filter, and the owner or an administrator can change the Owner.

docs.title: Internal filters
docs.text:
An internal filter is a set of conditions (If) and actions (Then). For each request in the script, the filter checks the conditions, and if they match, applies the actions to the request.

If All / Any of these conditions match a request: choose whether every condition must match, or at least one.

Each condition has:

  • the part of the request to look at: Hostname, Path, Query String or Post data;
  • the test: Contains, Does not contain, Starts with, Matches (a regular expression), Exist or Does not exist;
  • the value to test for.

Each action has a type, a part of the request to act on, and the inputs that part needs (a key, a value, or both):

Type Parts it acts on Remove the whole request, a request header, a query string parameter, a request cookie, or post data Replace a request cookie, request header, query string parameter or post data value; a validation; an assignment; the on-failure action; the path; the host Add a response data check, a validation, an assignment, a think time, a sleep time, a request cookie, a request header, a query string parameter, or post data

For validation actions, choose the check (Equals, Not equals, Contains and so on) before the value. For the on-failure action, choose one of the on-failure actions, apart from Goto specified group, which filters can't use.

Example

A filter with the condition Hostname Contains doubleclick and the action Remove the request removes every request to DoubleClick from a recording.

docs.title: External filters
docs.text:
An external filter runs a script, for changes an internal filter can't express. Choose the script under External script; Edit script opens it.

External scripts are listed under Filters › External filters. There you can create, open, download and delete them:

  • New external script starts from a template that shows how a filter receives the script being filtered (ioBean.getInput('script')) and changes its steps.
  • The Name must end in .js for the controller to run it as JavaScript. See Scripting languages for the languages a controller can run and the objects a script can use.
  • Test it runs the script, as edited, against one of your scripts and shows the changes it would make to the steps and its output. Nothing is saved.

You need the Create Script right to create external scripts. You can also write and test them on your own machine with the Script Filter Editor in the supplemental tools.

docs.title: Creating a filter group
docs.text:
1. Click New group.
  2. Enter a Name, and optionally choose a Product.
  3. Under Filters, tick the filters that belong to the group. Search narrows the list.
  4. Click Create.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Creating filters and groups needs the Create Filter right. Changing or deleting someone else's filter or group needs Edit Filter or Delete Filter; you can always change and delete your own. Applying filters to a script needs the right to edit that script. See Roles and permissions.

docs.title: Functions and Variables
docs.text: Variables and functions make a script dynamic: they put different data into each request, for each virtual user, while the test runs. They're evaluated on the agent.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
A variable is a named string. You can set one:
