  • In the project, as a global variable on the project's Variables tab (see Projects). Unless you allow scripts to override project variables, a script step can't change them.
  • With a Variable step in a script (see Scripts). The value can be a literal, an expression or a function.
  • With an assignment on a request, which stores part of the response (body, header or cookie) in a variable.
  • From a Logic step, with setVariable(name, value) (see Scripting Languages).

Each virtual user has its own copy of every variable. Tank also sets these:

Variable Description THREAD_ID The number of the virtual user on its agent. It can't be overridden. TANK_HTTP_PROXY Not set by Tank. If you set it to host:port, the agent sends requests through that proxy, for example myProxyserver:80.

docs.title: Using variables and functions
docs.text:
There are two ways to use a variable, and two to call a function.

Syntax Where it works Example #{expression} Anywhere in a value, any number of times. Use this. #{rootContext}/ajax/logEmail @name Only when it is the whole value. Replaced by the value of variable name. @webserver in a request's Host #function.category.name.arg1.arg2 Only when it is the whole value. The legacy function syntax, described below. #function.date.currentDate.yyyy-MM-dd

#{...} expressions are evaluated in request hosts, paths, protocols and ports, query strings, POST data and request bodies, headers, cookies, validations, assignments, authentication fields, think and sleep times, and Variable steps.

${...} isn't evaluated

Older guides show ${name} as an alternative to #{name}. Tank no longer evaluates it: ${name} is sent as the literal text ${name}. Use #{name}.

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
The text between #{ and } is a JEXL expression. Inside it:

  • A bare name is a variable: #{userName}. Use letters, digits and underscores in names you refer to this way; #{user-name} would mean user minus name.
  • Strings are quoted with ' or ": #{stringFunctions.concat('Intuit ', 'Tank')}.

  • Functions are called as category.function(arguments), and arguments can be variables or other function calls:

    #{stringFunctions.toBase64(ioFunctions.getFileData(fileName))}

    Here fileName is a variable whose value is passed to getFileData, whose result is passed to toBase64.

  • + joins strings and ? : chooses between values: #{env == 'prod' ? 'api.example.com' : 'qa.example.com'}.

For example, with a variable authId set to 51, #{numericFunctions.mod(authId, 10)} returns 1, and #{stringFunctions.concat('Intuit ', 'Tank ', 'Rocks')} returns Intuit Tank Rocks.

Keep these rules in mind:

  • An expression must produce a string. All the built-in functions return strings, apart from ioFunctions.getFileBytes. Arithmetic such as #{count + 1} produces a number and fails the step; use #{numericFunctions.add(count, 1)}.
  • Errors give an empty string. An unknown variable, a misspelled function or wrong arguments evaluate to "" rather than stopping the test. If a value comes out empty, check the spelling against the function pages.
  • An expression ends at the first }, so it can't contain a literal }.
  • When an expression is evaluated matters. A Variable step evaluates its value once, when the step runs: a variable set to #{stringFunctions.getUUID()} keeps the same UUID until it is set again. An expression written straight into a request field is evaluated every time the request runs.
  • Only Tank's functions can be called. Java methods on values, such as #{name.toUpperCase()}, aren't allowed and return an empty string.

docs.title: Built-in functions
docs.text: Category What it does ioFunctions Read values from CSV data files, and read whole files. stringFunctions Join, cut, encode and decode strings; random strings, UUIDs and user IDs. dateFunctions The current date and time, in any format and time zone. monetaryFunctions Random money amounts. numericFunctions Arithmetic and random numbers. taxFunctions Social Security Numbers.

docs.title: Legacy #function syntax
docs.text:
Before #{...} expressions, Tank called functions with a dotted syntax: #function.<category>.<name>.<arg1>.<arg2>.... It still works, and a few functions are only available this way, but prefer #{...} for new scripts. The rules:

  • The value must start with #function, and the function is the whole value; it can't be combined with other text.
  • Category and function names aren't case sensitive.
  • Arguments are separated by .. To put a dot inside an argument, write -dot-: #function.date.currentDateTime.HH:mm:ss-dot-SSS.
  • An argument that starts with @ is replaced by that variable's value: #function.string.concat.user-.@THREAD_ID. This doesn't work for the numeric functions or monetary.randomNegative, whose arguments must be literal numbers.
  • A function that fails, or a value that isn't a valid function, gives an empty value.
Function Description #function.date.currentDate.<format> Today's date in the agent's time zone. #function.date.currentDateTime.<format> The current date and time. Default format yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss. #function.date.currentUTC.<format> The current UTC time. Accepts the named UTC formats; default ISO 8601. #function.date.addDays.<days>.<format> The date days days from today (negative to go back). #function.date.addDaysUTC.<days>.<format> The UTC date and time days days from now. Accepts the named UTC formats; default ISO 8601. Example: #function.date.addDaysUTC.1.ISO_UTC. #function.monetary.randomPositive.<length> A random positive amount with length whole digits and two decimals. #function.monetary.randomNegative.<length> A random negative amount. #function.numeric.add.<v1>.<v2>... The sum of the values, as a decimal (#function.numeric.add.1.2.3 gives 6.0). Write decimals with -dot-. #function.numeric.subtract.<v1>.<v2>... The first value minus the others, as a decimal. #function.numeric.mod.<value>.<modulo> value % modulo. #function.numeric.randomPositiveWhole.<length> A random whole number with length digits. #function.numeric.randomNegativeWhole.<length> Its negative. #function.numeric.randomPositiveFloat.<length>.<decimals> A random number with length whole digits and decimals decimal places. #function.numeric.randomNegativeFloat.<length>.<decimals> Its negative. #function.string.concat.<v1>.<v2>... The arguments joined together. #function.string.substring.<subject>.<start>[.<stop>] Part of subject from start (inclusive) to stop (exclusive, optional). #function.string.substring.<startMarker>.<endMarker> In a body assignment or body validation only: the text of the response body between the first startMarker and the next endMarker (to the end of the body if endMarker isn't found). Used when the second argument isn't a number. Example: #function.string.substring.token=.& #function.string.lastSubstring.<startMarker>.<endMarker> Like the response-body substring, but starts at the last startMarker. Useful for the final event of a streamed response. #function.string.userid.<prefixLength>.<format> A random letters-and-digits prefix followed by today's date, like stringFunctions.userIdDate. #function.string.randomAlphaLower.<length> Random lower-case letters. #function.string.randomAlphaUpper.<length> Random upper-case letters. #function.string.randomAlphaMixed.<length> Random letters. #function.string.randomNumeric.<length> Random digits. #function.string.randomSpecial.<length> Random special characters. #function.string.randomAlphaMixedNumeric.<length> Random letters and digits. #function.string.randomAlphaMixedSpecial.<length> Random letters and special characters. #function.string.randomAlphaMixedNumericSpecial.<length> Random letters, digits and special characters. #function.string.useridFromRange.<min>.<max>[.<patterns>] A unique number from min (inclusive) to max (exclusive), split between agents like stringFunctions.userIdFromRange. Numbers matching any of patterns are skipped. #function.string.useridFromRangeExclude.<min>.<max>.<patterns> The same as useridFromRange with patterns. #function.string.useridFromRangeInclude.<min>.<max>.<patterns> As useridFromRange, but only numbers that match one of patterns. #function.string.useridFromRangeWithMod.<min>.<max>.<mod> As useridFromRange, but only multiples of mod. #function.string.useridFromRangeWithModInclude.<min>.<max>.<mod> The same as useridFromRangeWithMod. #function.string.useridFromRangeWithModExclude.<min>.<max>.<mod> As useridFromRange, but only numbers that aren't multiples of mod. #function.generic.getcsv.<column> Column column (zero-based) of the next line of csv-data.txt, read the same way as ioFunctions.getCSVData. Empty when the file runs out. #function.generic.getfiledata.<fileName>.<column> Column column of the next line of fileName. Dots in the file name can be written as-is. #function.generic.getssn[.<startSsn>] The next valid Social Security Number, unique across all agents: the range from startSsn (default 100000000) to 899999999 is split between the agents. #function.tax.getssn The next valid Social Security Number after the value of the variable SSN_START, like taxFunctions.getSsn. Empty if SSN_START isn't set. #function.datatype.<name> A boundary value for testing input validation. See the table below.

patterns for the useridFromRange functions are comma-separated Java regular expressions, each matched against the whole number: #function.string.useridFromRangeInclude.1000.2000.1[0-4]\d\d gives numbers from 1000 to 1499. Write any . in a pattern as -dot-.

The datatype names are BYTE_Max, BYTE_Min, BYTE_Max_Plus, BYTE_Min_Minus, SHORT_Max, SHORT_Min, SHORT_Max_Plus, SHORT_Min_Minus, INT_Max, INT_Min, INT_Max_Plus, INT_Min_Minus, LONG_Max, LONG_Min, LONG_Max_Plus and LONG_Min_Minus: the largest or smallest value of the Java type, or one beyond it. For example, #function.datatype.SHORT_Max_Plus gives 32768.

Warning

INT_Max_Plus and INT_Min_Minus overflow: they give -2147483648 and 2147483647 rather than 2147483648 and -2147483649.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Agent An instance, usually an EC2 instance started for the job, that runs a share of a job's virtual users and reports back to the controller. Agents exist for the length of a test. Agent Tracker The page that shows running and recent jobs and their agents, and controls them. See Jobs. API token A secret that lets tools and scripts call the REST API as you. Created on your account page. Assignment A rule on a request that copies a value from the response (body, header or cookie) into a variable. Controller The central server: it serves the web UI and the REST API, stores projects and scripts in its database, and starts and coordinates agents. Data file A file of test data, usually CSV, that scripts read with ioFunctions. Its lines are divided among a job's agents. See Data files. External filter A filter that runs a script (an external script) to change a script's steps. See Filters. Filter A rule, or a script, applied to a recorded script to remove, change or add to its requests. See Filters. Filter group A named set of filters applied together. Group (Of users) A role, such as user or project-manager, that grants rights. See Roles and permissions. (Of requests) A label shared by requests in a script, which on-failure actions and Logic steps can skip or jump to. Harness XML The form of a script or project that agents run. Downloadable from the Scripts page and the Agent Tracker. Job One run of a project: a snapshot of the project, queued, then run on agents. See Jobs. Logging key The name a request's (or a timer's) timings are reported under. Logic step A script step that runs JavaScript to change variables or control the flow of the test. Project The definition of a load test: users and times, test plans, data files, variables and job settings. See Projects. Ramp time How long a test takes to reach full load. Script The list of steps a virtual user runs. See Scripts. Script group An ordered, looped set of scripts within a test plan. It is a self-contained flow for a user, and a point where a stopped user can finish. Simulation time How long a test runs. Stop behavior Where users finish when a job is stopped: after the current step, script, script group, or the whole test. Tank Proxy The recording tool: a proxy that records a browser session as XML to create a script from. Test plan Part of a project that runs a percentage of the users, made of script groups. Timer A pair of script steps that times the steps between them as one transaction. TPS Transactions (requests) per second. Two-step start A job setting that starts every agent first and waits for Start load before applying load. Validation A check on a request's response. When it fails, the request's on-failure action applies. Variable A named value used in steps, set by a Variable step, an assignment, a Logic step or the project. Virtual user One simulated user, running a test plan's scripts on an agent.

docs.title: IO Functions
docs.text:
ioFunctions read the data files attached to a project. Files are read from the agent's data file directory.

Function Description Example getCSVData() Same as getCSVData(0, false): column 0 of the default data file, csv-data.txt. #{ioFunctions.getCSVData()} getCSVData(columnIndex) Same as getCSVData(columnIndex, false). #{ioFunctions.getCSVData(2)} getCSVData(columnIndex, loop) Column columnIndex (zero-based) of the current line of csv-data.txt. Set loop to true to start again at the first line when the file runs out. #{ioFunctions.getCSVData(1, true)} getCSVData(fileName) Same as getCSVData(fileName, 0, false). #{ioFunctions.getCSVData('users.csv')} getCSVData(fileName, columnIndex) Same as getCSVData(fileName, columnIndex, false). #{ioFunctions.getCSVData('users.csv', 1)} returns the second column getCSVData(fileName, columnIndex, loop) Column columnIndex (zero-based) of the current line of fileName. loop: true to go back to the first line after the last one is read. #{ioFunctions.getCSVData('users.csv', 1, true)} getFileData(fileName) The whole file as a string. The file is read once per agent and cached. An empty string if the file doesn't exist. #{ioFunctions.getFileData('body.json')} getFileBytes(fileName) The whole file as a byte array (byte[]). It isn't a string, so use it only as the argument of a function that takes bytes, such as stringFunctions.byteArrayToBase64. #{stringFunctions.byteArrayToBase64(ioFunctions.getFileBytes('logo.png'))}

docs.title: How CSV lines are read
docs.text:
• Each virtual user has its own current line in each file. Lines are handed out in order, so no two users on an agent get the same line.
  • Read each column of a line once. When a user asks for a column it has already read on its current line (or one past the end of the line), it moves on to the next line. Reading columns 0, 1 and 2 in turn gives the three values of one line; reading column 0 twice gives the first value of two lines.
  • Lines are split on every comma. Quoted values with commas in them aren't supported.
  • When the file runs out and loop is false, the virtual user is stopped (the agent logs CSV file (...) has no more data.).

Variables as arguments

Arguments can be variables or other functions: #{ioFunctions.getCSVData(dataFile, 0, true)} reads the file named by the variable dataFile.

The legacy #function.generic.getcsv and #function.generic.getfiledata forms are listed under Legacy #function syntax.

docs.title: Jobs and the Agent Tracker
docs.text: A job is one run of a project. Queueing a job takes a snapshot of the project, so you can keep editing the project without changing a job that is queued or running. When the job runs, the controller starts agents, each running a share of the virtual users, and they report back to the controller as the test runs.

docs.title: Running a test
docs.text:
1. In the project editor, set the job settings on the Create job tab.
  2. Click Validate and queue…, check the summary, errors and warnings, and click Queue job. The job is created with the status Created and appears on the Job queue tab.
  3. Click the job's Run button. The controller launches the agents (EC2 instances, or the registered agents of a standalone controller) and the job becomes Starting, then Running once the agents report in.
  4. With Two-step start, the agents start and wait. Once they are connected and ready, click Start load to begin the test.

You can queue, run and control a project's jobs if you own the project or have the Control Job right (see Roles and permissions).

docs.title: The Agent Tracker
docs.text:
Agent Tracker in the menu bar shows the jobs of every project with activity in the last seven days, grouped by project. A project's Job queue tab shows the same view for that project only.

The toolbar has:

  • View: how to look at the jobs (below). Your choice is remembered in this browser.
  • Show finished jobs: include jobs that have ended.
  • Refresh now, and Refresh every 10, 15, 30, 60 or 120 seconds, or off.
  • Columns (table view): show or hide columns.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
View Shows Table A tree of projects, their jobs and each job's agents. Columns: name, ID, status, WebSocket state, region, active users, target users, TPS, failures, CPU, memory, heap, started and completed. Heat map Every agent as a tile, job by job and region by region, shaded by the figure you pick (TPS, active users, failures, time since last seen, CPU, memory, heap or JVM threads), so a slow, failing or silent agent stands out. A tile opens that agent's figures and actions. Metrics Agent host and JVM health from Amazon CloudWatch: fleet averages, a CPU chart of the busiest agents, and a row per agent with CPU, memory, heap, JVM thread, GC and TCP connection charts. Jobs A card per job: users against target, TPS and its trend, failures, its agents at a glance, and its actions. Regions Agents by AWS region and availability zone: how many are running, paused, starting, lost or finished, with their users, TPS and jobs. Timeline Jobs as bars from start to end over the last 6 hours, 24 hours or 7 days, coloured by status, so overlapping runs and gaps are easy to see.

CPU, memory and JVM figures come from CloudWatch, where the controller collects them; agents that don't report them show n/a.

docs.title: Job details and charts
docs.text:
The chart button on a job (or a job's name) opens its details: status, who created it and when, start and end times, active and total users, and failure counts (kills, aborts, restarts, gotos, skips and group skips). It also shows the job's settings as they were queued, and charts of active users by script and TPS over time, including the TPS of each request. For a single agent, the chart button shows that agent's TPS.

A project's row has a button to download its Harness XML, the file the agents run.

docs.title: Controlling a job
docs.text:
The buttons on a job or agent row change with its state. Only the actions the job or agent can take at the moment are shown.

Action Applies to What it does Run job Starts a job that is Created. Start load job For a two-step job that is Starting: begins the load once the agents are ready. Pause ramp job, agent Stops adding users and holds the current level; users already running carry on. Resume ramp job, agent Continues adding users. Pause job, agent Stops adding users and interrupts the running users. Resume job, agent Lets users run and ramp again. Stop job, agent Asks users to finish and stop, at the point set by the job's Stop behavior: after the current step, script, script group, or the whole test. Kill job, agent Terminates the agents immediately, without letting users finish. Tank asks you to confirm. Delete job Removes a job that hasn't started (Created).

Actions are sent to the agents asynchronously, so the status can take a few seconds to change. The tracker refreshes straight after an action, and again shortly after.

docs.title: Job states
docs.text:
Status Meaning Created Queued and waiting to be run. Starting Agents are being launched or, for a two-step job, are waiting for Start load. Running The test is running. RampPaused Running, but no more users are being added. Paused Paused. Stopped Stopped by a user. Completed Finished, or killed. Aborted Couldn't start, for example when a standalone controller has no agents available. Deleted Deleted before it ran. Deleted jobs aren't shown.

An agent's status (such as pending, starting, ready, running, stopping, terminated) and its WebSocket state are shown on its row. An agent that has disconnected mid-run is shown as lost.

If agents don't start or report in time, the controller's watchdog restarts them, up to a limit the administrator sets (the watchdog section of settings.xml); after that it kills the job.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
While a job runs, the Agent Tracker shows live active users, TPS and failures for each project, job and agent, and the job details show users and TPS over time.

Agents also send their TPS and per-request timing results to the reporting provider configured on the controller (the reporting section of settings.xml). The default configuration writes them to Amazon CloudWatch, under the Intuit/Tank namespace, where you can chart and keep them. A request's logging key decides which name its timings are reported under, and a timer reports a set of steps as one transaction. The job's logging profile controls how much the agents log about each request.

docs.title: Automating jobs
docs.text: Everything here is also available through the REST API. Create an API token on your account page to queue, start, check and stop jobs from CI.

docs.title: Monetary Functions
docs.text:
monetaryFunctions generate random money amounts with two decimal places. length is the number of digits before the decimal point.

Function Description Example randomPositive(length) A random positive amount. #{monetaryFunctions.randomPositive(3)} returns e.g. 225.08 randomNegative(length) A random negative amount. #{monetaryFunctions.randomNegative(3)} returns e.g. -225.08

These are shorthand for numericFunctions.randomPositiveFloat(length, 2) and numericFunctions.randomNegativeFloat(length, 2), and produce digits the same way (see Numeric Functions).

docs.title: Numeric Functions
docs.text: numericFunctions do arithmetic and generate random numbers. Arguments can be numbers, numeric strings or variables holding numbers, and every result is a string.

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text: Function Description Example add(values...) Adds any number of values. The result is a decimal. #{numericFunctions.add(3, 2, 6)} returns 11.0 subtract(values...) Subtracts the second and later values from the first. The result is a decimal. #{numericFunctions.subtract(10, 2, 3)} returns 5.0 mod(value, modulo) The remainder of whole-number division value % modulo. #{numericFunctions.mod(authId, 10)} returns 1 when authId is 51 toInt(value) Drops the fractional part of a number. Useful to turn the result of add or subtract into a whole number. #{numericFunctions.toInt(numericFunctions.add(1, 2))} returns 3

docs.title: Random numbers
docs.text:
Function Description Example random(max) A random whole number from 0 (inclusive) to max (exclusive). #{numericFunctions.random(10)} returns 0 to 9 random(min, max) A random whole number from min (inclusive) to max (exclusive). Returns 0 if max isn't greater than min. #{numericFunctions.random(4, 10)} returns 4 to 9 randomPositiveWhole(length) A random whole number with length digits. An empty string if length is 0. #{numericFunctions.randomPositiveWhole(3)} returns e.g. 427 randomNegativeWhole(length) The negative of randomPositiveWhole(length). #{numericFunctions.randomNegativeWhole(3)} returns e.g. -427 randomPositiveFloat(length, decimalPlaces) A random number with length digits before the decimal point and decimalPlaces after it. #{numericFunctions.randomPositiveFloat(3, 2)} returns e.g. 427.15 randomNegativeFloat(length, decimalPlaces) The negative of randomPositiveFloat(length, decimalPlaces). #{numericFunctions.randomNegativeFloat(3, 2)} returns e.g. -427.15

Digits used by the randomPositive* and randomNegative* functions

These functions build the number one digit at a time: the first digit is 1–8 and each later digit is 0–8. The digit 9 never appears, so randomPositiveWhole(3) returns a value from 100 to 888. Use random(min, max) when you need every value in a range.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
A project describes a load test: how many virtual users to run, how fast to add them and for how long, which scripts they run, which data files and variables the scripts can use, and how the test's agents are set up. You run a project by queueing a job from it; see Jobs and the Agent Tracker.

A project holds:

Project
├── Users and times      workload type, ramp, simulation time, users by region
├── Test plans           each runs a share of the users
│   └── Script groups    run in order, each looped
│       └── Scripts      run in order, each looped
├── Data files
├── Variables
└── Job settings         logging, HTTP client, stop behavior, agents

docs.title: The project list
docs.text:
Open Projects in the menu bar. The list is paged and sorted on the server, and its state (page, sort, search) is kept in the address, so a reload or the browser's Back button brings you back to the same view.

  • Search matches the name, product and comments.
  • All owners narrows the list to one owner; My projects is your own.
  • Columns shows or hides columns. Column choices and widths are saved for you; reset them on your account page.
  • Each row can be opened, copied under a new name, or deleted. Tick several rows to delete them together.

docs.title: Creating a project
docs.text:
1. Click New project.
  2. Enter a Name (it must be unique), and optionally choose a Product and add Comments. Products are a list the administrator configures, used to categorize projects and scripts.
  3. Click Create. Tank creates the project with one test plan, Main, which runs 100% of the users, and opens it.

You need the Create Project right to create or copy a project (see Roles and permissions).

docs.title: The project editor
docs.text:
The top of the editor has the project's Name, Product, Owner and Comments. Only the owner or an administrator can change the owner.

Below them are six tabs: Users and times, Scripts, Data files, Variables, Create job and Job queue. Changes to the first five are kept in the page until you click Save; the title shows (unsaved) until then, and Tank warns you if you try to leave with unsaved changes.

  • Save checks the project first. If something is wrong, the problems are listed and the tabs that have them are marked with a count.
  • Revert throws away unsaved changes.
  • Save as… saves the project under a new name, with your unsaved changes; the original stays as it was last saved.
  • The trash button deletes the project.

If someone else saved the project while you were editing it, Tank tells you and offers to reload it.

If you can't edit the project, it opens read-only with a note saying so.

docs.title: Users and times
docs.text:
Setting Description Workload type Increasing (linear user ramp) adds users in steps over the ramp time, then holds them. Non-linear (target users per second) injects new users at a rate that rises from 0 to a target rate over the ramp time. Simulation time How long the test runs. Required when Run scripts until is Simulation time is reached. Ramp time How long it takes to reach full load. Initial users Users started as soon as the test starts. Usually 0. User increment (Increasing only) Users added at each step of the ramp. Usually 1. With 3,000 users, a 15 minute ramp and an increment of 1, about 3.33 users are added each second. Run scripts until (Increasing only) Simulation time is reached, or Scripts finish: each user runs its test plan, with its loops, once. Target users per second (Non-linear only) The rate new users are injected at by the end of the ramp. Users by region (Increasing) The number of users to run in each region. Total users adds them up. Share of users by region (Non-linear) The percentage of users each region runs.

The regions are the AWS regions the administrator has configured. On a standalone controller there is a single, standalone region.

Times are written with d, h, m, s and ms, for example 1h 30m or 90m. A time can also refer to the other times: RT (ramp time), ST (simulation time) and ET (execution time), as in 3ET - .5RT. A region's users can be an expression too, such as 4 * RT / 1000 for four users a second. Separate math symbols with spaces.

docs.title: Scripts: test plans and script groups
docs.text:
The Scripts tab sets the flow of the test.

  • A test plan runs a percentage of the test's users. Every project has at least one. Tank warns you if the percentages don't add up to 100%.
  • A test plan contains script groups, which run in order. A script group is a self-contained flow for a user and has its own Loop count. Script groups are also where a stopped user can finish (see Stop behavior below).
  • A script group contains scripts, which run in order, each with its own Loop count.

To work with them:

  • Add test plan adds a plan with a name and user percentage; each plan is a tab. Delete test plan removes a plan and its groups.
  • Add script group adds a group at the end; the insert button on a group's row adds one before it. Each row can also be edited or deleted.
  • In the script group dialog, set the group's Name and Loop, find scripts under Add scripts (by name, product or comments) and click Add. Use the arrows to reorder the scripts, set each script's Loop, or remove it. Click Done, then save the project.

Loops

Script Group 1 loops twice and contains Script1 (looped once) and Script2 (looped twice). Each user runs: Script1, Script2, Script2, Script1, Script2, Script2

docs.title: Data files
docs.text:
The Data files tab lists the data files the project's scripts can read.

  • Find a file under Add data files and click Add.
  • Upload data files uploads new files and adds them to the project.
  • The eye button previews a file; the remove button takes it out of the project (the file itself is kept).

When a job runs, each data file's lines are divided evenly among the job's agents. If the job has exactly one data file, it is the default file that #{ioFunctions.getCSVData(column)} reads.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Project variables are set for every user of every script in the project. Click Add variable and enter a name and value. Each name can be used once.

By default a script can't change a project variable. Turn on Let scripts override project variables to let scripts set their own values.

Sending requests through a proxy

Set a variable named TANK_HTTP_PROXY to proxyHost:proxyPort, for example myProxyServer:80, to make the agents send requests through that proxy.

See Functions and variables for how scripts use variables.

docs.title: Create job
docs.text:
The Create job tab holds the settings a job is made with, and queues the job. The settings are saved with the project.

Setting Description Job name Leave it blank for the default name. Logging profile How much the agents log about each request: Terse, Standard, User Variables (standard plus user variables), Verbose (every field) or Trace Calls (every call). HTTP client The HTTP client implementation the agents use to drive load. The administrator configures the choices. Stop behavior Where users finish when the job is stopped: after the current Step, Script, Script Group, or the whole Test. Location Where the test runs from, for information. The administrator configures the choices. Agent instance type The EC2 instance type for the agents. Choosing a type fills in its default users per agent. Not shown on a standalone controller. Users per agent (Increasing) How many users each agent runs, which decides how many agents the job starts. Target rate per agent (Non-linear) How many users per second each agent injects. Assign Elastic IPs Gives each agent an unassigned Elastic IP in its region. Not shown on a standalone controller. Two-step start Launches every agent first and waits for Start load, so load begins at an exact moment, for example in a spike test. Send Start load within 5 to 10 minutes of the agents being ready.

Click Validate and queue…. Unsaved changes are saved first. Tank then shows what the job will be (users, ramp time, simulation time and expected run time) with any errors to fix and warnings to check. If the job is valid, click Queue job. The job is a snapshot of the project as it is now, so later edits to the project don't change it. Tank then opens the Job queue tab.

You need the Control Job right, or to own the project, to queue a job.

docs.title: Job queue
docs.text: The Job queue tab shows this project's jobs and their agents, and lets you run, pause, stop or kill them. It is the same view as the Agent Tracker, limited to one project.

docs.title: Scripting Languages
docs.text:
Two parts of Tank run code you write: Logic steps in a script, and external filters. Both use the Java scripting API (JSR 223) and talk to Tank through an object called ioBean.

Logic step External filter script Runs on The agent, each time a virtual user reaches the step The controller, when the filter is applied to a script Language JavaScript only Chosen by the file name's extension: .js JavaScript, .groovy Groovy, .rb Ruby Inputs (ioBean.getInput(name)) variables, request (the previous request), response (the previous response) script, the script being filtered Outputs (ioBean.setOutput(name, value)) action, which controls the flow of the test (see Logic) none; change the script object instead

docs.title: Available engines
docs.text:
• JavaScript (the Nashorn engine) is always present, on the agent and on the controller.

  • Groovy and Ruby (JRuby) are only bundled when Tank is built with the script-engines Maven profile:

    mvn clean install -P release,script-engines

    That adds them to tank.war (for external filter scripts) and to the Tank-Script-Runner-all.jar tool. The agent never has them, so Logic steps are always JavaScript.

Note

The web UI tests external scripts in a sandboxed JavaScript engine, so it can only test .js external scripts, even on a controller built with Groovy and JRuby. Groovy and Ruby filters still run when the filter is applied.

docs.title: The ioBean object
docs.text: Method Description getInput(name) One of the inputs listed above, or null. setOutput(name, value) / getOutput(name) Sets or reads an output value. println(text), print(text) Writes to the script's output. debug(text), error(text) Writes at debug or error level.

docs.title: Logic steps
docs.text:
Before a Logic step runs, Tank adds helper functions in front of it: log, logWithDate, debug, error, toJsonObj, toJsonString, getRequest, getResponse, getResquestBody (spelled as shown), getResponseBody, getVariable, setVariable, gotoGroup, restartPlan, abortScriptGroup, abortScript, abortGroup, terminateUser and setAction. Logic describes each one. An administrator can change them in the logic-step section of the controller's settings.xml.

getVariable and setVariable work on the same variables as the rest of the script. The variables input also has an evaluate method, which runs #{...} expressions, so a Logic step can call the built-in functions:

var vars = ioBean.getInput("variables");
var id = vars.evaluate("#{stringFunctions.getUUID()}");
setVariable("requestId", id);

docs.title: External filter scripts
docs.text:
An external filter script gets the script being filtered as script and edits it in place. Its list of steps can't be changed directly: copy it, change the copy and set it back.

var script = ioBean.getInput("script");
var steps = new (Java.type("java.util.ArrayList"))(script.getSteps());
ioBean.println(script.getName() + " has " + steps.size() + " steps");
script.setSteps(steps);

You can develop and run filter scripts outside Tank with the Script Runner tool (tools/script_filter_pkg/target/Tank-Script-Runner-all.jar), which offers every language it was built with.

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
A script is the list of steps a virtual user runs during a load test. A project puts scripts into script groups and test plans, and every user runs them in that order.

A step is one of:

Step What it does Request Sends an HTTP or HTTPS request, then validates the response and saves values from it into variables. Think time Pauses for a random time between a minimum and a maximum, like a user reading a page. Sleep time Pauses for a fixed time. Variable Sets a variable to a value or a function. Cookie Sets a cookie (name, value, domain and path). Authentication Supplies credentials (user name, password, realm, host, port and scheme: Basic, Digest or NTLM). Clear session Clears cookies and the cache, like closing and reopening the browser. Logic Runs JavaScript to change variables or control the flow of the test. Timer A pair of start and stop markers that time the steps between them as one transaction.

docs.title: The script list
docs.text:
Open Scripts in the menu bar. Like the project list, it is paged, searchable (by name, product and comments), can be narrowed to one owner, and remembers your columns.

Each row can be opened, copied under a new name, downloaded as Tank XML (the script itself, for importing elsewhere) or as Harness XML (the form the agent runs), or deleted.

docs.title: Creating a script
docs.text:
There are three ways to get a script into Tank:

  • Record a browser session with the Tank Proxy and create a script from the recording.
  • Start a blank script and add steps by hand.
  • Import a script exported from Tank.

docs.title: Importing a recorded script
docs.text:
1. Record a session with the Tank Proxy. It saves the traffic as XML.
  2. On the Scripts page, click New script and choose From a recording.
  3. Enter a Name, and optionally choose a Product.
  4. Under Recording, choose the XML file the proxy saved (.xml, or gzipped .gz).
  5. Under Filters to apply, tick the filter groups and filters to clean up the recording with. Ticking a group ticks its filters; you can then untick any you don't want. The filters run in list order.
  6. Click Create. Tank creates the script and opens it.

docs.title: Starting a blank script
docs.text: Click New script, keep Blank script, enter a Name and optionally a Product and Comments, and click Create.

docs.title: Importing Tank XML
docs.text:
Click Import Tank XML and choose one or more scripts exported from Tank: .xml files, gzipped .gz files, or a .zip of them. Each file replaces the script with the ID and name it carries; a file with an ID of 0 creates a new script. If some files fail, the dialog stays open and lists which.

You need the Create Script right to create, copy or import scripts.

docs.title: The script editor
docs.text:
The editor shows the script's Name, Product and Comments, then its steps. As in the project editor, changes are kept in the page until you click Save; Revert discards them. Save as… copies the saved script under a new name (save or revert your changes first). The header also has links to download the script as Tank XML and Harness XML.

If you can't edit the script, it opens read-only.

docs.title: Working with steps
docs.text:
• Add step adds a step of the chosen type. It goes before the selected step, or at the end when none is selected.
  • Click a step's Data cell, or its Edit button, to open it.
  • Tick steps to Copy them. Paste puts copied steps before the selected step, in this script or another one. Copied steps last until you reload the page.
  • Drag steps to reorder them, or select them and use Move to… to move them to a position. Scripts with more than 300 steps scroll virtually and can only be reordered with Move to….
  • Timer group wraps the selected steps in a timer. The timer's name is the logging key its timing is reported under.
  • Delete selected removes the ticked steps. Deleting either half of a timer removes both.
  • Columns chooses which columns show: index, group, request name, method, protocol, host, path, data, MIME type, logging key, on failure, comments, validation and assignment.

docs.title: Script tools
docs.text:
• Search finds steps by text in the parts you choose: any request field, URL, host, path, method, request name, group, logging key, MIME type, query string, post data, request and response headers and cookies, response content, think and sleep times, and variable names and values. * matches any text. You can then replace the matches, in the ticked steps, in all steps, or one step at a time with a preview. Replacing is an unsaved change like any other.
  • Apply filters runs filters over the script's steps. The result is an unsaved change.
  • Validate checks the script: the expected time for one pass through it, the data files it reads, and warnings such as variables that are used but never set, or set but never used.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variables hold values used to parameterize requests, such as host names, query strings and post data. A variable can be set:

  • by a Variable step, to a literal value or a function;
  • by a request's assignments, from its response;
  • by a Logic step;
  • by the project.

Refer to a variable in a later step as @name (for example a host of @{host}). See Functions and variables for the full syntax.

Sending requests through a proxy

Set a variable named TANK_HTTP_PROXY to proxyHost:proxyPort, for example myProxyServer:80, to make the agent send requests through that proxy.

docs.title: Think time and sleep time
docs.text:
Think time simulates a user's pause between pages: Tank waits a random time between the Minimum and Maximum. Sleep time waits a fixed time.

Both are in milliseconds. Instead of a number you can use a variable (@delay), a function (#function...) or an expression (#{...}).

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
A request has:

Field Description Name An optional label, such as Login. Group Requests with the same group name form a group that the on-failure actions can skip or jump to. Optional. Method GET, POST, PUT, DELETE or OPTIONS. Protocol http or https. Host A host name or IP address, optionally with :port. It can use variables, such as @{host}. Path The path of the resource. It can use variables and functions. On failure What the user does when a validation fails (see below). Logging key Groups this request's timings in the results.

Its tabs hold:

  • Headers: the request headers, as key and value pairs.
  • Query string: parameters added to the URL.
  • Post data: the request body, as Key-Value pairs, XML, JSON (with a Format JSON button), Plain Text, or Multi-Part. A recorded multipart body is shown as recorded and can't be edited.
  • Validations: checks on the response (see below).
  • Assignments: values to copy from the response into variables.
  • Recorded: what the recording captured: the cookies sent, the response headers and cookies, and the response body.

Headers that aren't replayed

The agent always sends a TEST: LoadTest header. It doesn't replay these recorded headers: Host, Cookie, Connection, Content-Type, Content-Length, If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. To send one anyway, prefix its name with X-Include- (for example X-Include-If-None-Match); the prefix is removed when the request is sent.

Recorded request cookies are only replayed when their value is a variable (starts with @).

docs.title: Validations
docs.text:
Each validation has:

  • When: After the request (the usual case) or Before the request.
  • Location: the response Body, a Header or a Cookie.
  • Lookup: for the body, a JSON path (such as $.status) or an XPath (such as /cart/id), depending on the Response format (JSON, XML or RAW); for a header or cookie, its name.
  • Operator: Equals, Not equals, Is empty, Is not empty, Contains, Does not contain, Less than, Greater than or Equals any.
  • Value to compare with, where the operator needs one.

A lookup of HTTPRESPONSECODE checks the HTTP status code (such as 200 or 404), and HTTPRESPONSEMESSAGE the status message (such as OK or Not Found).

docs.title: Assignments
docs.text: Each assignment has a Location (Body, Header or Cookie), the Variable to set, and the Lookup to read, as for validations.

docs.title: On failure
docs.text:
When a validation fails, the user does one of:

Action Description Abort script, goto next script (default) Skips the rest of the script and goes to the next script in the project. Abort script group goto next script group Skips to the next script group. Skip remaining requests in group Goes to the step after the last request in this request's group. Continue to next request Carries on. Goto specified group Jumps to the first step of the group you name. Terminate user Stops this virtual user. Restart user Starts this user's test plan again.

docs.title: Clear session
docs.text: Clears the user's cookies and cache, as if the browser were closed and reopened.

docs.title: Logic
docs.text:
A Logic step runs JavaScript on the agent, between requests. Use it to change variables, control the flow of the test, or do anything too complex for the other steps. The editor's What can a script use? button shows the code Tank runs before your script.

A Logic step can read:

  • variables: the current user's variables;
  • request: the previous request;
  • response: the previous response.

It controls the flow by setting the action output on ioBean, which the functions below do for you:

Action Effect goto <groupName> Jumps to the group with that name in the script. restartPlan Restarts the test plan from the start. abortScriptGroup Aborts the current script group and goes to the next one. abortScript Aborts the current script and goes to the next one. abortGroup Aborts the current group of requests and goes to the request after it. terminateUser Stops the current user.

Test it runs your script on the controller against test data you enter (variables, a request and a response), or against the step's previous request with Use the previous request, and shows the result. See Scripting languages for more on the ioBean object.

These functions are added in front of every Logic step. An administrator can change them in the logic-step section of the controller's settings.xml.

Functions added to every Logic step LoggingData transformationData retrievalFlow control 
/** Prints the line, with the date, to the output. */
function logWithDate(line) {
    ioBean.println(new Date().toString + ": " + line);
}

/** Prints the line to the output. */
function log(line) {
    ioBean.println(line);
}

/** Prints the line at error level. */
function error(line) {
    ioBean.error(line);
}

/** Prints the line at debug level: shown when testing, not logged in production. */
function debug(line) {
    ioBean.debug(line);
}

function toJsonObj(text) {
    try {
        return JSON.parse(text);
    } catch(e) {
        error("Error parsing json: " + e);
    }
    return text;
}

function toJsonString(jsonObj) {
    try {
        return JSON.stringify(jsonObj, null, '\t');
    } catch(e) {
        error("Error converting json to string json: " + e);
    }
    return jsonObj;
}

/** The com.intuit.tank.http.BaseRequest of the last call, or null if none was made. */
function getRequest() {
    return ioBean.getInput("request");
}

/** The com.intuit.tank.http.BaseResponse of the last call, or null if none was made. */
function getResponse() {
    return ioBean.getInput("response");
}

/** The request body as a string, or "" if there is none. (The name is spelled as shown.) */
function getResquestBody() {
    if (getRequest() != null) {
        return getRequest().getBody();
    }
    return "";
}

/** The response body as a string, or "" if there is none. */
function getResponseBody() {
    if (getResponse() != null) {
        return getResponse().getBody();
    }
    return "";
}

/** The variable's value, or null if it doesn't exist. */
function getVariable(key) {
    return ioBean.getInput("variables").getVariable(key);
}

/** Sets the variable. */
function setVariable(key, value) {
    ioBean.getInput("variables").addVariable(key, value);
}

/** Jumps to the group with this name; if there is none, skips to the next script. */
function gotoGroup(groupName) {
    setAction("goto " + groupName);
}

/** Restarts the test plan from the start. */
function restartPlan() {
    setAction("restartPlan");
}

/** Aborts the current script group and goes to the next. */
function abortScriptGroup() {
    setAction("abortScriptGroup");
}

/** Aborts the current script and goes to the next. */
function abortScript() {
    setAction("abortScript");
}

/** Aborts the current group and goes to the request after it. */
function abortGroup() {
    setAction("abortGroup");
}

/** Stops this user. */
function terminateUser() {
    setAction("terminateUser");
}

/** Sets the action output. */
function setAction(action) {
    ioBean.setOutput("action", action);
}

docs.title: String Functions
docs.text: stringFunctions build, cut, encode and generate strings.

docs.title: Building and cutting strings
docs.text: Function Description Example concat(values...) Joins any number of strings. #{stringFunctions.concat('Intuit ', 'Tank', ' Rocks')} returns Intuit Tank Rocks substring(subject, start) subject from index start (zero-based) to the end. #{stringFunctions.substring('hello world', 6)} returns world substring(subject, start, stop) subject from start (inclusive) to stop (exclusive). A stop of -1 or past the end means "to the end". #{stringFunctions.substring('hello world', 0, 5)} returns hello substringBetween(subject, open, close) The first string found between open and close. #{stringFunctions.substringBetween('yabcz', 'y', 'z')} returns abc substringBetween(subject, open, close, index) The index-th (zero-based) string found between open and close. If open is null, returns everything before the first close; if close is null, everything after the last open. Empty if there is no match. #{stringFunctions.substringBetween('yabcz ydefz', 'y', 'z', 1)} returns def replaceBetween(subject, open, close, replace, encodeData) Replaces the text between the first open and the next close with replace, keeping open and close. A null open or close means the start or end of subject. With encodeData true, subject is Base64-decoded first and the result is Base64-encoded again. #{stringFunctions.replaceBetween('a[b]c', '[', ']', 'X', false)} returns a[X]c

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text: Function Description Example toBase64(toEncode) Base64-encodes a string. #{stringFunctions.toBase64('ab')} returns YWI= fromBase64(toDecode) Decodes a Base64 string (as UTF-8). #{stringFunctions.fromBase64('YWI=')} returns ab byteArrayToBase64(bytes) Base64-encodes a byte array, such as the result of ioFunctions.getFileBytes. #{stringFunctions.byteArrayToBase64(ioFunctions.getFileBytes('logo.png'))} urlEncode(toEncode) URL-encodes a string (UTF-8, application/x-www-form-urlencoded). #{stringFunctions.urlEncode('a b&c')} returns a+b%26c urlDecode(toDecode) URL-decodes a string (UTF-8). #{stringFunctions.urlDecode('a+b%26c')} returns a b&c

docs.title: Random strings and IDs
docs.text:
Each length is the number of characters to generate.

Function Characters used Example randomAlphaLower(length) a–z #{stringFunctions.randomAlphaLower(8)} randomAlphaUpper(length) A–Z #{stringFunctions.randomAlphaUpper(8)} randomAlphaMixed(length) a–z, A–Z #{stringFunctions.randomAlphaMixed(8)} randomNumeric(length) 0–9 (may start with 0) #{stringFunctions.randomNumeric(4)} randomSpecial(length) !@#$%^*{[}]:;,.?~` #{stringFunctions.randomSpecial(4)} randomAlphaMixedNumeric(length) letters and digits #{stringFunctions.randomAlphaMixedNumeric(8)} randomAlphaMixedSpecial(length) letters and special characters #{stringFunctions.randomAlphaMixedSpecial(8)} randomAlphaMixedNumericSpecial(length) letters, digits and special characters #{stringFunctions.randomAlphaMixedNumericSpecial(8)} getUUID() A random UUID. #{stringFunctions.getUUID()} returns e.g. 6a244e4f-d4ea-4a7b-8882-73ca5c729527 Function Description Example userIdDate(prefixLength, format) A random prefix of prefixLength letters and digits followed by today's date in format (a Java SimpleDateFormat pattern). #{stringFunctions.userIdDate(4, 'yyyy-MM-dd')} returns e.g. GdGE2011-11-15 on November 15, 2011 userIdFromDate(prefixLength, format) Same as userIdDate. #{stringFunctions.userIdFromDate(4, 'yyyy-MM-dd')} userIdFromRange(minId, maxId) A unique whole number from minId (inclusive) to maxId (exclusive). The range is split evenly between the agents, and each agent hands out its share in random order, each number once. When an agent's share runs out the function returns an empty string. #{stringFunctions.userIdFromRange(1, 1000)}

Note

An expression ends at the first }, so an argument can't contain a literal }: #{stringFunctions.substringBetween(body, '{', '}')} doesn't work. Store } in a variable (say closeBrace) and pass that instead: #{stringFunctions.substringBetween(body, '{', closeBrace)}.

The legacy #function.string... forms, including the useridFromRange variants with include/exclude patterns and the response-body substring, are listed under Legacy #function syntax.

docs.title: Tax Functions
docs.text:
taxFunctions generate test data for tax applications.

Function Description Example getSsn(startSsn) The next valid Social Security Number, formatted NNN-NN-NNNN. The first call on an agent starts at startSsn; every later call on that agent, from any virtual user, returns the next valid number after the previous one (later startSsn values are ignored). Numbers outside the issued SSN ranges are skipped. #{taxFunctions.getSsn(1010001)} returns 001-01-0001, then 001-01-0002, ...

Known limitations

  • The sequence isn't split between agents, so two agents started with the same startSsn return the same numbers. For numbers that are unique across agents, use the legacy #function.generic.getssn.<startSsn>, which gives each agent its own share of the range.
  • A nine-digit startSsn (100000000 or more) gives a malformed result: getSsn(562000000) returns 056-20-0000. Start below 100000000, or use #function.generic.getssn.

See Legacy #function syntax for #function.generic.getssn and #function.tax.getssn.

docs.title: The Web UI
docs.text: Tank's web UI is served at the controller's root, for example https://tank.example.com/ (or https://tank.example.com/tank/ if the war is deployed as tank.war rather than ROOT.war). It talks to the controller through the same REST API that tools and CI pipelines use.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text: Sign in with your Tank user name and password, or with Sign in with SSO when the controller has single sign-on configured. After signing in you return to the page you asked for (the project list by default). When your session expires, Tank asks you to sign in again.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
The menu bar runs across the top of every page:

Section What it's for Projects Create and edit projects, and queue and run their jobs. Agent Tracker Watch and control running and recent jobs and their agents. Scripts Create, import and edit scripts. Filters Manage filters, filter groups and external filter scripts. Data files Upload and manage data files. Tools Download the desktop tools. Admin Users, logs and the log level. Only administrators see it; see Administration.

On the right are your user name, which opens your account page, Help, and Sign out. The Tank logo opens the home page, which outlines the path from a recording to a running test and links to each section. If the administrator has set a banner, it shows above the menu bar. The controller's version is in the footer.

docs.title: Lists and editors
docs.text:
The Projects, Scripts and Data files lists work the same way:

  • Search, an owner filter (My projects, My scripts and so on), sorting and paging, all kept in the page address so you can bookmark or share a view.
  • Columns to choose what shows. Column choices and widths are saved for you.
  • Row buttons to open, copy, download or delete, and checkboxes to delete several items at once.
  • Buttons are disabled, with a tooltip, when you don't have the right to use them.

The project, script and filter editors share these behaviors:

  • Changes are kept in the page until you click Save. (unsaved) shows in the title until then, and Tank warns you before you leave with unsaved changes.
  • Revert discards your changes; Save as… saves a copy under a new name.
  • If someone else saved the item while you were editing it, Tank tells you and offers to reload it.
  • Items you can't change open read-only.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: The Tools page downloads the tools that run on your own machine: the Agent visual debugger, the Script filter editor, the Tank Proxy recorder and the API test harness. They need Java 17 or later, and are only included when the controller was built with the release profile. See Supplemental tools.

docs.title: Your account
docs.text:
Click your user name to open your account page. There you can:

  • see your user name, groups and when you last signed in;
  • change your email;
  • change your password (used for signing in with a user name and password, not for SSO);
  • create, replace or delete your API token. Tools, the Jenkins plugin and scripts use it to call Tank as you, with the header Authorization: Bearer <token>. Tank shows a new token once, so copy it straight away;
  • Reset preferences, which puts every table's columns and widths back to their defaults.

docs.title: Help
docs.text: Help links to these docs, the REST API documentation (Swagger UI), and, on a release build, the guides bundled with the controller and the Javadoc for the classes external filter scripts work with. It also shows the controller's build version.

docs.title: The classic UI
docs.text:
The previous JSF user interface is still available under /classic, for example https://tank.example.com/classic/. It shares your session, so you don't need to sign in again. Old bookmarks to JSF pages (addresses ending in .jsf) redirect to the same page under /classic, and links from when the React UI was served under /app redirect to the same page at the root.

The classic UI is kept for compatibility; these docs describe the main UI.
